# Xecute complete documentation


---

# Learn Xecute

Documentation route: /docs

Build a Rust API with a clear home for routes, input validation, application logic,
and data access. Xecute adds a CLI, modules, and dependency injection on top of
Axum, so you can start with a connected feature instead of wiring everything first.

You do not need a database to get started. You should be comfortable running
terminal commands and reading basic Rust structs and async functions.

## New to Xecute? Follow this path

| Step | What you will do | Guide |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | Install the CLI, run an API, and send a valid and invalid request | [Build your first API](skills/xecute/references/getting-started/quickstart.md) |
| 2 | Generate `/user`, change a validation rule, and run tests | [Your first feature](skills/xecute/references/getting-started/first-feature.md) |
| 3 | Follow input from the HTTP route to storage | [How a request works](skills/xecute/references/getting-started/request-flow.md) |
| 4 | Add your own body, URL, and query inputs | [Controllers and extractors](skills/xecute/references/http/controllers.md) |
| 5 | Share providers between features | [Providers and modules](skills/xecute/references/architecture/modules.md) |

Start with MVC, the default. Learn [CQRS](skills/xecute/references/architecture/mvc-cqrs.md) when you want
to separate write operations from read operations. You can use the same concepts
without adding a message bus or a second database.

## Already building something?

| I need to… | Go to |
| --- | --- |
| Understand generated files | [Project structure](skills/xecute/references/architecture/project-structure.md) |
| Find a CLI command | [CLI reference](skills/xecute/references/cli/commands.md) |
| Move from NestJS | [Coming from NestJS](skills/xecute/references/getting-started/coming-from-nestjs.md) |
| Configure a port, limits, or environment | [Application configuration](skills/xecute/references/configuration/application.md) |
| Test a route or replace a dependency in tests | [Testing modules and HTTP](skills/xecute/references/testing/modules.md) |
| Connect PostgreSQL | [PostgreSQL](skills/xecute/references/integrations/postgres.md) |
| Protect routes | [Guards and JWT](skills/xecute/references/integrations/auth.md) |
| Fix a setup or startup problem | [Troubleshooting](skills/xecute/references/operations/troubleshooting.md) |
| Update an existing generated application | [Adoption guide](skills/xecute/references/getting-started/adopting-existing.md) |

## Add capabilities when you need them

Lifecycle management is part of the runtime. Database, JWT authentication, jobs,
caching, and CQRS buses are enabled through Cargo features and explicit provider
configuration. Start with the generated API, then follow the integration guide for
each capability. The [feature setup guide](skills/xecute/references/getting-started/status.md) explains
what is generated and what you configure yourself.

A generated resource starts with collection GET and create POST, validation, and
an **in-memory** repository. It does not create login, database persistence,
update/delete endpoints, background workers, or cache configuration automatically.

## A few terms you will see

| Term | Plain meaning |
| --- | --- |
| Feature | One part of your application, such as users or orders |
| DTO | A Rust struct describing accepted request data and validation rules |
| Provider | An object registered so Xecute can inject it where needed |
| Module | A group of providers, with explicit imports and exports |
| Repository | The part that reads and writes data |
| Lifecycle | Startup and shutdown work, such as opening and closing a pool |

Tutorials tell you where to run commands and what to expect. Reference pages cover
the available APIs in more detail. The source link at the bottom identifies where
the page is maintained; it is useful when you want to inspect implementation details.

---

# Build your first API

Documentation route: /docs/getting-started/quickstart

By the end of this guide, you will have a running Rust API, create a record, and
see it in a response. Start with MVC; you can learn CQRS after your first feature.

## 1. Check your tools

You need Rust **1.98.1 or newer**, Cargo, rustfmt, and Clippy. Generated projects
pin Rust 1.98.1 in `rust-toolchain.toml`.

```sh
rustc --version
cargo --version
rustup component add rustfmt clippy
```

No database, Redis, or authentication provider is needed for this tutorial.
The generated repository stores records in memory.

## 2. Install Xecute

Run this from any directory:

```sh
cargo install xecute-cli --version 0.1.20 --locked
xecute --version
```

The version command should print `xecute 0.1.20`. If the command is missing, check
that Cargo’s `bin` directory is on your `PATH`. To replace an existing CLI install,
add `--force` to the install command.

## 3. Create a project

Run this from the directory where you keep your projects:

```sh
xecute new my-api
cd my-api
```

This creates an MVC application and an `example` feature. MVC means your HTTP
controller calls a service, and the service calls a repository. You do not need
to wire the generated example yourself.

The generator resolves a fresh `Cargo.lock` using the latest
compatible dependencies. Keep that file in Git. A network failure leaves the
project files available; enter the project and retry `cargo generate-lockfile`.
Breaking dependency versions are not automatically adopted.

## 4. Start the server

Keep this terminal open:

```sh
xecute run dev
```

The first build can take longer because Cargo downloads and compiles dependencies.
The default server address is `http://127.0.0.1:3000`. The development runner
watches source files and rebuilds when you save a change. Use `cargo run` if you
prefer a single run without watching.

Open `http://127.0.0.1:3000/docs/` for your application’s Swagger UI. This is the
API documentation generated by your app, separate from this Xecute learning site.

## 5. Send your first requests

Open a **second terminal**. Keep the server running in the first one.

```sh
curl -i http://127.0.0.1:3000/example
```

Expect `200 OK` and an empty collection. Now create a record:

```sh
curl -i -X POST http://127.0.0.1:3000/example \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"name":"My first record"}'
```

Expect `201 Created` and a record containing a generated UUID and your name.
Run the GET request again to see the saved record. The generated middleware may
wrap response data; use Swagger to inspect the response contract.

Records disappear when the server restarts. You have not connected a database yet.

## 6. Try an invalid request

```sh
curl -i -X POST http://127.0.0.1:3000/example \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"name":"A"}'
```

Expect `422 Unprocessable Entity`. Names must contain 3–100 characters and cannot
be whitespace only. Xecute checks the DTO before calling the controller method;
you do not add a manual validation call to the handler.

## If something does not work

| What you see | What to do |
| --- | --- |
| `xecute: command not found` | Check Cargo’s bin directory in `PATH`, then reopen the terminal |
| Downloads or dependency resolution fail | Check registry/network access; run `cargo generate-lockfile` in the generated app |
| Port 3000 is already in use | Stop the other server or change the listener configuration in `config/AppConfig.toml` |
| POST returns `415` | Add `Content-Type: application/json` |
| POST returns `422` | Use the `name` field with 3–100 nonblank characters; remove unknown fields |
| GET is empty after saving code | The watcher restarted the app, clearing the in-memory repository |

## Next: build your own feature

Continue with [Your first feature](skills/xecute/references/getting-started/first-feature.md). You will
generate `/user`, find the right files, change a rule, and run the generated tests.

---

# Your first feature

Documentation route: /docs/getting-started/first-feature

You already have a running example API. Now add a `user` feature and learn which
file to change for each kind of work. This guide follows an MVC project created
in the [quick start](skills/xecute/references/getting-started/quickstart.md).

## 1. Generate the feature

In a terminal at your **application root**, beside `Cargo.toml`, run:

```sh
xecute g resource user
```

`g` is short for `generate`. A resource creates the connected files and registers
the module and its routes. You do not need to add the generated router manually.
If the development server is running, wait for its rebuild to finish.

The route is singular: `/user`, not `/users`.

## 2. Find the files you will use

```text
src/modules/user/
├── module.rs           # Registers providers and exports the service
├── controller.rs       # HTTP routes and request/response handling
├── service.rs          # Coordinates application operations
├── dto/mod.rs          # Accepted request fields and validation
├── entity/mod.rs       # The record returned by your feature
├── repository/store.rs # Stores and retrieves records
└── tests/http.rs       # Tests requests through the feature router
```

A DTO describes input. An entity represents a record. A repository owns data
access. A service coordinates the work. The controller connects HTTP to that work.
For a complete directory map, see [Project structure](skills/xecute/references/architecture/project-structure.md).

## 3. Create and list a user

With the server running:

```sh
curl -i -X POST http://127.0.0.1:3000/user \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"name":"Munna"}'

curl -i http://127.0.0.1:3000/user
```

Expect `201 Created` for POST and `200 OK` for GET. The collection should contain
the new user. The generated repository is in memory, so restarting clears it.

The generator provides **list and create**. Get-by-ID, update, delete, pagination,
login, and database persistence are not generated endpoints.

## 4. Follow one request

```text
POST /user
  → dto/mod.rs: decode and validate CreateUserDto
  → controller.rs: call UserService
  → service.rs: trim the name and call UserRepository
  → repository/store.rs: save the record
  → controller.rs: return 201 and the record
```

Open these files in this order. Notice that the controller has an
`Arc<UserService>` field: Xecute injects the registered service. The service has
an `Arc<UserRepository>` field for the same reason.

## 5. Change a validation rule

Open `src/modules/user/dto/mod.rs`. The generated name rule currently allows
3–100 characters. Change the maximum from `100` to `50` in **both** attributes:

```rust
#[schemars(length(min = 3, max = 50))]
#[validate(length(min = 3, max = 50), custom(function = "non_blank"))]
```

This is an attribute fragment: replace the two attributes on the existing `name`
field, keeping its type and the generated `non_blank` function.

`validate` enforces the rule at runtime. `schemars` describes it in the API schema.
Keeping both in sync makes Swagger match what the server accepts.

Save the file and wait for the rebuild. Send a 51-character name:

```sh
curl -i -X POST http://127.0.0.1:3000/user \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"name":"123456789012345678901234567890123456789012345678901"}'
```

Expect `422`. A valid name such as `Munna` should still return `201`.

## 6. Run the tests

From the application root:

```sh
cargo test user
cargo fmt --all -- --check
```

The generated HTTP tests cover the feature router. Add a test for your new
51-character rejection beside those tests; check the status and verify that
invalid input did not create a record. See [Testing modules and HTTP](skills/xecute/references/testing/modules.md)
for request assertions and provider overrides.

## Where should my next change go?

| I want to… | Start here |
| --- | --- |
| Accept another JSON field | `dto/mod.rs`; then pass it through the service and storage as needed |
| Add a URL parameter or query filter | `controller.rs` and a DTO in `dto/mod.rs` |
| Add an application operation | `service.rs` |
| Change how data is saved | `repository/store.rs` |
| Use a provider from another feature | `module.rs` imports and the owning module’s exports |
| Protect a route | [Guards and JWT](skills/xecute/references/integrations/auth.md), following its feature setup |

## Using CQRS instead?

In a new project, select CQRS before generating resources:

```sh
xecute new query-api --cqrs
cd query-api
xecute g resource user
```

The controller calls `CreateUserHandler` and `ListUserHandler` instead of a
`UserService`. Look in `commands/create.rs` and `queries/list.rs`. DTOs, repositories,
and HTTP validation follow the same ideas. Read [MVC and CQRS](skills/xecute/references/architecture/mvc-cqrs.md)
when you want to understand that choice.

Next, learn [How a request works](skills/xecute/references/getting-started/request-flow.md) and then
[Controllers and extractors](skills/xecute/references/http/controllers.md).

---

# How a request works

Documentation route: /docs/getting-started/request-flow

Use this page as a map when reading generated code. You need only the
[example application](skills/xecute/references/getting-started/quickstart.md) to follow along.

## The five pieces

| Piece | Its job | Example in the user feature |
| --- | --- | --- |
| DTO | Describe and validate request data | `CreateUserDto` accepts a name |
| Controller | Match an HTTP route and return a response | POST `/user` calls the service |
| Service or handler | Coordinate one application operation | Normalize input and ask the repository to save |
| Repository | Read and write data | Save a record in the generated in-memory store |
| Module | Register providers and control visibility | Make the service available for injection |

Dependency injection (DI) means Xecute creates registered objects and passes their
dependencies through typed fields. `Arc<UserService>` is a shared reference to a
service, not a new service constructed for every call.

## Example: a valid POST

1. The server receives POST `/user` with a JSON body.
2. Server middleware applies configured HTTP policies.
3. The route extractor decodes `CreateUserDto` and checks its validation rules.
4. The controller calls the service (MVC) or command handler (CQRS).
5. The operation calls the repository, which creates a record.
6. The controller returns `201 Created` with that record; response middleware can wrap it.

```text
MVC:  HTTP → DTO → Controller → Service → Repository
CQRS: HTTP → DTO → Controller → Command/Query Handler → Repository
```

A GET list request has no JSON body to validate. Its query parameters are only
validated if you add a query DTO and use `#[query]`.

## Example: an invalid POST

Send `{"name":"A"}` to a generated create endpoint. JSON decoding succeeds,
but name validation fails. You receive `422` before the controller method or
repository runs. A malformed JSON document instead returns `400`; a missing JSON
content type returns `415`.

This validation belongs to HTTP extraction. Calling a service directly in Rust
does not automatically validate a DTO. Enforce business invariants in your
application/domain logic wherever they are required.

## Decide where a value comes from

| Request value | Handler input | Example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| JSON body | `#[body] payload: CreateUserDto` | POST body `{"name":"Munna"}` |
| URL segment | `#[param] id: u64` | `/user/42` with `#[get("/{id}")]` |
| Query string | `#[query] query: SearchQuery` | `/user?limit=10` |
| Headers | `headers: axum::http::HeaderMap` | Read `Authorization` or another header |
| URL-encoded form | `form: axum::extract::Form<ContactForm>` | HTML form submission |
| Raw text or bytes | `String` or `axum::body::Bytes` | A plain-text or binary body |

These are parameter fragments, not extra routes already generated by the CLI.
Put reusable DTO structs in `dto/mod.rs`; import them into the controller.
`#[body]` and `#[query]` DTOs need `Deserialize`, `Validate`, and `JsonSchema`.
A form DTO needs `Deserialize`; form validation must be called explicitly.

Use only one body-consuming extractor per handler, placed last. JSON, forms,
raw text, raw bytes, and multipart all consume the request body. Headers, path,
and query values can be used alongside that one body extractor.

## What a module import does

If `OrderService` needs `UserService`, the user module must export `UserService`
and the order module must import the user module. Both module definitions must
be registered in the application graph.

An import grants visibility; it does not automatically discover modules or mount
routes. The resource generator handles registration for generated features.
Manual assembly needs explicit definitions and routers.

Next, use [Controllers and extractors](skills/xecute/references/http/controllers.md) for handler code,
[DTO validation](skills/xecute/references/http/validation.md) for rules, or
[Providers and modules](skills/xecute/references/architecture/modules.md) for cross-feature injection.

---

# Features and setup

Documentation route: /docs/getting-started/status

Xecute gives you a working API first. Add database access, authentication,
background processing, caching, and buses as your application needs them.
Most integrations are opt-in so you control dependencies and configuration.

## What is generated and what do I configure?

| Capability | Generated behavior | Your setup |
| --- | --- | --- |
| MVC resources | Controller → service → repository | Default; add your application logic |
| CQRS resources | Controller → handler → repository | Choose `--cqrs` when creating the project |
| Request validation | Create DTO in `dto/mod.rs` | Add fields and validation rules |
| Search/path/form inputs | Input examples in controller comments | Add DTOs and route handlers |
| Module imports | Imports section and usage guide | Export shared providers and register module definitions |
| Lifecycle | Synchronous startup helpers | Use async startup and cleanup for async resources |
| PostgreSQL | In-memory repository | Enable `postgres`; configure pool, migrations, SQL repository |
| JWT authentication | Public resources | Enable `auth`; configure trusted verification and guards |
| Background jobs | No worker created automatically | Enable `jobs`; register queue, handlers, and shutdown |
| Caching | No automatic response caching | Enable `cache` or `cache-redis`; define keys and TTLs |
| CQRS buses/events | Direct handler calls | Enable `cqrs`; register buses and handlers |

## Enable a capability

For example, enable authentication and CQRS buses in your application manifest:

```toml
[dependencies]
xecute = { version = "0.1", features = ["auth", "cqrs"] }

[dev-dependencies]
xecute = { version = "0.1", features = ["testing"] }
```

Merge the flags with your existing dependency declaration. In a Cargo workspace,
set the version in `[workspace.dependencies]` and select features on inherited
application dependencies. Keep `Cargo.lock` committed for reproducible builds.

Feature flags expose APIs. They do not create credentials, connect external
services, replace repositories, or protect routes automatically. Follow the
[feature reference](skills/xecute/references/reference/features.md) and the relevant integration guide.

## Updating an existing application

Updating the CLI changes the executable used for future generation. It does not
rewrite existing source files or migrate application startup.

Use the [adoption guide](skills/xecute/references/getting-started/adopting-existing.md) to add capabilities
one at a time, including provider registration, startup, shutdown, and tests.

---

# Upgrade an existing application

Documentation route: /docs/getting-started/adopting-existing

Enable and integrate one capability at a time, keeping the application compiling
and its existing HTTP tests passing. Installing a newer CLI does not rewrite app
files; this guide covers the explicit migration work.

## 1. Enable the runtime features

In a standalone app, merge the required flags into the existing runtime dependency:

```toml
[dependencies]
xecute = { version = "0.1", features = ["auth", "postgres", "jobs", "cache-redis", "cqrs"] }
```

Choose only the flags you use. For memory caching select `cache` rather than
`cache-redis`. Async lifecycle needs no extra feature. Keep the app's test-only
`testing` feature in dev-dependencies where appropriate.

For a generated workspace, update the shared dependency once:

```toml
# Workspace Cargo.toml
[workspace.dependencies]
xecute = { version = "0.1" }

# apps/my-api/Cargo.toml
[dependencies]
xecute = { workspace = true, features = ["auth", "cqrs"] }
```

Merge these fields with the existing manifests rather than replacing unrelated
dependencies/lints. Run `cargo generate-lockfile` and commit the resulting lockfile
with your application's dependency changes. `--runtime-path` affects generated
projects; it does not install or select a different CLI executable.

## 2. Move resource initialization to an async path

Generated `AppModule::container()` is synchronous. Add an async helper alongside
it using the existing `definitions()` registry:

```rust
pub async fn container_async() -> Result<Container, InjectError> {
    let container = ModuleGraph::new(Self::definitions()).build()?;
    container.initialize_async().await?;
    Ok(container)
}
```

Use `AppModule::container_async().await?` in server bootstrap, retain the returned
`Arc<Container>`, and call `router_with_container(container.clone())` after startup
completes. Router assembly remains synchronous once resources are ready.

Retain the generated configuration, shared policies, version/docs routers and
request draining. Refactor the existing post-initialization work into an async
block returning a Result; afterward await `container.shutdown_async()` on success
or failure, then propagate the results. The complete
[async lifecycle guide](skills/xecute/references/architecture/lifecycle.md) and runnable examples show
cleanup ownership. Account for early router/listener setup failures too.

Application tests calling the old sync helper need an async setup path when their
registrations include async factories or lifecycle hooks. Use
`TestingModule::compile_async().await` for isolated provider tests.

## 3. Register resources and enforce module visibility

A generated `#[module]` provides static type registrations. Build its definition,
then append configured provider definitions where needed:

```rust
let definition = UserModule::definition().provider(configured_provider);
```

Here `configured_provider` is a `ProviderDefinition` built from your validated
configuration. Include this definition once in `AppModule::definitions()`. For a
shared database/cache module, export the concrete provider type, import its owning
module in consumers, and include all module definitions in the graph.

Do not register a configured provider twice or re-register an imported service in
every module. Factories must declare the dependencies they resolve. The container
validates duplicates, cycles, module visibility and unsafe lifetime capture.

## 4. Adopt each capability

| Capability | App changes | Verification |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Lifecycle | Async factories and `on_init`/`on_shutdown` registration methods | Startup order, failed setup cleanup and shutdown |
| PostgreSQL | Pool config, migration provider, SQL repository, readiness | Run against dedicated PostgreSQL; verify commit/rollback |
| Authentication | Trusted verifier, controller/route guards and explicit policies | Missing/invalid JWT → 401; insufficient permissions → 403 |
| Jobs | Typed payload, bounded queue and handler; dependency-aware cleanup | Retry, overload handling and drain accepted work |
| Cache | Cache-aside reads and post-write invalidation | TTL, tenant/user key separation, storage failures |
| CQRS buses | Message/handler traits, bus registration and controller mapping | One command/query handler, event failures and pipeline ordering |

Read the detailed [PostgreSQL](skills/xecute/references/integrations/postgres.md),
[auth](skills/xecute/references/integrations/auth.md), [jobs](skills/xecute/references/integrations/jobs.md),
[cache](skills/xecute/references/integrations/cache.md), and [CQRS](skills/xecute/references/integrations/cqrs.md) guides.
Use compiled example code as a reference; adapt repository and policy logic to
your own application's contracts.

## 5. Preserve the application boundary

Keep body/query/path/form DTOs under `dto/`; controller methods import them and
map requests to service calls, commands or queries. Put SQL in repositories,
workflow logic in services/handlers, and configured resources in DI definitions.
Protect private endpoints explicitly before using authorization-sensitive cache
keys. Queues and event buses are process-local; use durable delivery/outbox
infrastructure for work that must survive a process crash.

## Verify before deployment

Run the app's existing tests, add tests for each enabled capability, and check
formatting/Clippy. Verify generated-app tests against your selected runtime version, not only
the library's unit tests. The [example catalog](skills/xecute/references/testing/examples.md) provides
working commands and external-service requirements.

---

# Coming from NestJS

Documentation route: /docs/getting-started/coming-from-nestjs

Xecute uses Rust and Axum with explicit registration. Several architectural ideas
will be familiar, but NestJS decorator names do not imply matching runtime APIs.

| NestJS concept | Xecute implementation |
| --- | --- |
| Module imports/exports | `#[module(imports = [...], providers = [...], exports = [...])]` plus all definitions in `ModuleGraph` |
| Injectable provider | `#[derive(Injectable)]` or `#[injectable]` on a named-field struct |
| Constructor injection | Typed fields such as `Arc<UserRepository>` |
| Controller and HTTP methods | `#[controller]`, `#[routes]`, `#[get]`, `#[post]` and other verbs |
| Body/query/path inputs | `#[body]`, `#[query]`, singular `#[param]`; other Axum extractors directly |
| Validation pipe | Automatic JSON/query DTO decoding plus `validator` validation |
| Guards / UseGuards | `#[guard(...)]` on a module, controller, or route; async functions return `Result<Request, E>` |
| Authentication/authorization | Optional `auth` verifier, `AuthenticatedUser`, roles/permissions |
| Request scope | `Scope::Request`, `RequestScope` and scoped controller routers |
| Lifecycle | `singleton_async`, `on_init`, `on_shutdown`, explicit async startup/shutdown |
| CQRS buses | Optional typed `CommandBus`, `QueryBus`, `EventBus` and `Behavior` |
| Queues | Optional bounded in-process `JobQueue<T>`; not BullMQ/durable broker storage |
| Cache | Explicit TTL cache API; memory/LRU or Redis; no automatic HTTP interceptor |

## Choose the generated architecture

MVC uses `Controller → Service → Repository`. CQRS uses
`Controller → Command/Query Handler → Repository`. A focused domain service can be
used by handlers when reusable logic needs it; a forwarding service is not
mandatory. Buses are an additional explicit choice, not a requirement for CQRS.

## Important differences

Module imports establish visibility but do not auto-discover definitions or mount
routes. The CLI registers resource definitions and controller routers through
markers in `AppModule`; manual modules need both kinds of registration.

Guards follow nested Axum scopes: app middleware/guards wrap controller
middleware/guards, then route middleware/guards and extraction. This is documented
Xecute ordering, not a promise of NestJS's universal request lifecycle.

Lifecycle attribute markers such as `#[on_module_init]` remain placeholders.
Use the provider registration methods described in the lifecycle guide. There is
no built-in dynamic module registration convention, full HTTP interceptor system,
ORM entity decorators, session/login scaffold or persisted saga engine.

Rust APIs use concrete types and typed errors rather than reflection-based token
lookup. `Command` and `Query` traits declare Output/Error types; event subscribers
receive a shared `Arc<E>`. Explicit configuration and feature flags make startup
and deployment behavior inspectable.

Read [feature setup](skills/xecute/references/getting-started/status.md) before enabling integrations
and the [adoption guide](skills/xecute/references/getting-started/adopting-existing.md) when updating an
existing generated application.

---

# CLI reference

Documentation route: /docs/cli/commands

Use this page when you know what you want to generate and need the exact command or flag. Run resource generators beside your application’s Cargo.toml.

```text
xecute new <project|.> [--name <package-name>] [--mvc | --cqrs] [--runtime-path <path>]
xecute update
xecute uninstall
xecute run dev [--bin <name>] [--features <list>] [--watch <path>] [-- <app arguments>]
xecute generate <resource|module|controller|service> <name>
xecute g <res|mo|co|s> <name>
xecute --help
xecute --version
```

| Command | Result |
| --- | --- |
| `xecute new my-app` | MVC application with a working example resource |
| `xecute new .` | Initialize the current directory using its name as the package name |
| `xecute new . --name my-app` | Initialize the current directory with an explicit package name |
| `xecute update` | Install the latest crates.io CLI into the running CLI's Cargo installation root |
| `xecute uninstall` | Remove the Cargo-installed CLI; application projects are retained |
| `xecute new my-app --mvc` | Explicit MVC selection |
| `xecute new my-app --cqrs` | Application with command/query handlers |
| `xecute new my-project --workspace` | Cargo workspace with its first MVC application under `apps/` |
| `xecute g apps admin [--mvc \| --cqrs]` | Add an app from the workspace root; inherit architecture unless overridden |
| `xecute run dev` | Rebuild and restart the debug application when watched files change |
| `xecute g resource user` or `xecute g res user` | Resource, module registration, routes, schemas, repository, and HTTP test |
| `xecute g module billing` or `xecute g mo billing` | Registered module with an empty provider list |
| `xecute g controller status` or `xecute g co status` | Standalone injectable controller with a GET endpoint |
| `xecute g service mailer` or `xecute g s mailer` | Standalone injectable service |

Run generators from the generated project root. Standalone controllers and
services require manual provider/route registration when you decide to use them.
Standalone generators remain available in both architecture modes.

Names must start with a lowercase ASCII letter and contain lowercase letters,
digits, hyphens, or underscores. Rust keywords and empty name segments are
rejected. `user-profile` becomes the module `user_profile` and types such as
`UserProfileController`. Existing feature paths are not overwritten.

The CLI saves the architecture as `mvc` or `cqrs` in `.xecute/architecture`.
Commit this file. Subsequent resource generation follows that selection; projects
without it retain the legacy MVC layout. Invalid values stop generation.
Changing the file changes future generation, not existing feature code.

Keep the `// xecute:` registration markers in `src/app_module.rs`. Generators
use them to add module imports, container definitions, routes, and API metadata.

## Keep learning

[Development runner](skills/xecute/references/cli/development.md). Return to the [learning path](skills/xecute/references/index.md) whenever you need a different topic.

---

# Development runner

Documentation route: /docs/cli/development

Keep a development server running while you edit Rust files. Start with a generated application; this runner rebuilds and restarts it when watched files change.

With CLI 0.1.7 or later installed, run this from your application's directory:

```sh
xecute run dev
```

The CLI starts `cargo run` in the debug profile and monitors project files. Saving
source or configuration changes automatically stops the previous process, rebuilds,
and restarts the application. It uses Cargo's incremental build cache; there is
no separate watcher executable to install.

```sh
# Choose a binary in a project with several binary targets:
xecute run dev --bin server

# Also watch a local runtime or another source directory (repeatable):
xecute run dev --watch ../xecute/xecute --watch ../xecute/xmacros

# Pass arguments to the application, preserving individual argument boundaries:
xecute run dev -- --port 4000
```

The application must implement any arguments passed after `--`; the generated
server configures its port with `server.bind_address` in `config/AppConfig.toml` instead.

The watcher polls file metadata every 200 ms and groups edits with a 300 ms quiet
period. It detects additions, changes, removals, and rename-save operations for
Rust, TOML, JSON, YAML, SQL, HTML, CSS, JavaScript, TypeScript, and GraphQL files,
plus `Cargo.lock`, `.env`, and `.env.*`. An explicitly watched file can have any
extension. Additional watch paths must exist when the command starts. Files in
symlinked subdirectories are not followed; pass a real path with `--watch` if needed.

Cargo's resolved target directory is excluded, including custom
`CARGO_TARGET_DIR` settings. Directories named `target`, `.git`, `.hg`, `.svn`,
`node_modules`, `dist`, `build`, `.idea`, and `.vscode` are also excluded. Runtime
logs and ordinary data files are not watched unless their extension is in the
list above or they are explicitly selected. Keep generated JSON/configuration
output outside the watched source tree to avoid restart loops.

Compiler diagnostics and application logs remain visible in the terminal. A
failed build or exited app leaves the watcher running; saving another change
retries it. An edit during compilation cancels the old process before starting
the next build. If the project has multiple runnable binaries, select one with
`--bin`. Dependencies outside the project tree need explicit `--watch` paths.

Ctrl-C stops the watcher and its managed Cargo/application processes. On Unix,
restarts and shutdown send SIGTERM to the process group, allow up to five seconds
for cleanup, then force termination if necessary. On Windows, the process tree
is terminated with `taskkill /T /F`. Dev shutdown can therefore be shorter than
the generated server's normal production drain deadline. Application stdin is
closed; this command is intended for development servers, not interactive programs.

This is **rebuild-and-restart hot reload**: it restarts the server process, resets
in-memory data, and does not automatically refresh the browser or patch a running
process. Use `cargo run` for a single run and `cargo build --release --locked`
for a production binary. Hot reload runs only when explicitly using `xecute run dev`.

## Keep learning

[Cargo workspaces](skills/xecute/references/cli/workspaces.md). Return to the [learning path](skills/xecute/references/index.md) whenever you need a different topic.

# Cargo workspaces

Documentation route: /docs/cli/workspaces

Choose a workspace when several applications should share dependency declarations and repository tooling. A single application does not need this setup.

Workspace scaffolding is available starting with CLI 0.1.14. MVC is the default:

```sh
xecute new my-project --workspace
cd my-project
xecute g apps admin
xecute g apps billing --cqrs
xecute g apps dashboard --mvc
cargo build --workspace
cargo test --workspace
```

The first application is created at `apps/my-project/`. Each app keeps its own
configuration, HTTP server, feature modules, and MVC or CQRS architecture.
Applications share the root `Cargo.lock`, `target/`, and dependency definitions
in `[workspace.dependencies]`. App dependencies use `workspace = true`, with
features selected per app. New applications inherit
the workspace architecture; use `--mvc` or `--cqrs` to override it.
`xecute new my-project --workspace --cqrs` selects CQRS for the workspace.

Run resource generators and the development server inside an app:

```sh
cd apps/admin
xecute g resource user
xecute run dev
```

Configure distinct bind addresses in the apps' `config/AppConfig.toml` files
when running them together. See [the CLI workspace guide](https://github.com/morshedulmunna/xecute/blob/main/xecute-cli/README.md#multiple-applications-in-a-workspace)
for local runtime paths, container builds, and in-place initialization.

## Keep learning

[Update and uninstall](skills/xecute/references/cli/update.md). Return to the [learning path](skills/xecute/references/index.md) whenever you need a different topic.

---

# Update and uninstall

Documentation route: /docs/cli/update

Update the installed CLI executable or remove it. Updating the CLI does not rewrite an application you already generated.

For a CLI installed through Cargo:

```sh
xecute update
xecute uninstall
```

`update` runs `cargo install xecute-cli --registry crates-io --locked --force` in
the same installation root as the running executable. It updates the CLI and
its templates; it does not edit application dependencies or regenerate existing
projects. It requires Cargo and access to crates.io. A local/source installation
is replaced by the published registry version, which may not include unreleased
local features. Check the release status above before updating a development build.

`uninstall` runs `cargo uninstall xecute-cli` against that same root. It removes
the installed CLI, including installations created with `cargo install --root`.
It does not remove application directories, source code, or the Cargo toolchain.

The CLI verifies Cargo's `.crates2.json` installation metadata before invoking
these commands. Executables run directly from `target/debug` or copied outside a
registered installation are rejected with guidance to use Cargo directly.
Unix commands wait for Cargo and report failures. On Windows, a PowerShell helper
waits for the running executable to exit before starting Cargo; its terminal
output reports completion or errors after the CLI returns.

To initialize an existing directory without creating a nested folder:

```sh
mkdir my-api
cd my-api
xecute new .
xecute run dev

# Optional package name, architecture, and local runtime:
xecute new . --name my-api --cqrs --runtime-path /absolute/path/to/xecute/xecute
```

The final example is an alternative initialization command for an uninitialized
directory. The default package name comes from the current directory's basename;
use `--name` if the basename contains spaces, uppercase letters, or other invalid
characters. `--name` can also override a named project's Cargo package name.
MVC remains the default, and `--cqrs` selects CQRS.

In-place generation checks all scaffold destinations before writing. Conflicting
files such as `Cargo.toml`, `README.md`, or `.gitignore` cause a clear error with
no scaffold files changed. Move those conflicting files or choose a fresh directory
before retrying. Unrelated files and an existing `.git` directory are preserved.
Symlinked scaffold parents are rejected. Generation does not change the shell's
working directory and does not print an extra `cd` step for `new .`.

# Project structure

Documentation route: /docs/architecture/project-structure

Use this directory map to find the file you need to edit. Start in src/modules for feature work; use src/server for shared HTTP behavior.

A generated MVC project contains:

```text
my-app/
├── .xecute/architecture
├── config/
│   └── AppConfig.toml
├── .env.example
├── Cargo.toml
├── Cargo.lock
├── rust-toolchain.toml
├── rustfmt.toml
├── clippy.toml
├── deny.toml
├── Dockerfile
├── .github/workflows/ci.yml
└── src/
    ├── main.rs
    ├── app_module.rs
    ├── middleware.rs           # Global middleware hook
    ├── configs/               # Validated TOML settings and secret readers
    ├── server/
    │   ├── bootstrap.rs       # Listener and graceful shutdown
    │   ├── router.rs          # Shared HTTP policies and probes
    │   ├── docs.rs            # Swagger/OpenAPI endpoints
    │   ├── error.rs           # Public error envelope
    │   ├── health.rs
    │   ├── logging.rs
    │   ├── rate_limit.rs
    │   ├── shutdown.rs
    │   └── middleware/        # Built-in guards, logging, response handling
    ├── modules/
    │   ├── mod.rs
    │   └── example/
    │       ├── mod.rs
    │       ├── module.rs
    │       ├── controller.rs
    │       ├── service.rs
    │       ├── dto/mod.rs
    │       ├── entity/mod.rs
    │       ├── repository/
    │       │   ├── mod.rs
    │       │   └── store.rs
    │       └── tests/
    │           ├── mod.rs
    │           └── http.rs
    └── tests/                 # Shared server HTTP tests
```

Feature filenames are `controller.rs`, `module.rs`, and `service.rs`; the Rust
type names retain the feature prefix. Resource HTTP tests live in
`src/modules/<feature>/tests/http.rs`.

## Keep learning

[MVC and CQRS](skills/xecute/references/architecture/mvc-cqrs.md). Return to the [learning path](skills/xecute/references/index.md) whenever you need a different topic.

# MVC and CQRS

Documentation route: /docs/architecture/mvc-cqrs

MVC uses a service to coordinate operations. CQRS gives each read or write its own handler. Both use DTOs and repositories; start with MVC if you are unsure.

MVC is the default resource layout:

```text
Request → DTO validation → Controller → Service → Repository → Response
```

Create a CQRS project with:

```sh
xecute new my-api --cqrs
cd my-api
xecute g resource user
```

Its resource uses command/query handlers that inject the repository:

```text
src/modules/user/
├── controller.rs
├── module.rs
├── mod.rs
├── commands/
│   ├── mod.rs
│   └── create.rs    # CreateUserCommand + CreateUserHandler
├── queries/
│   ├── mod.rs
│   └── list.rs      # ListUserQuery + ListUserHandler
├── dto/mod.rs
├── entity/mod.rs
└── repository/
    ├── mod.rs
    └── store.rs
```

```text
POST → DTO validation → Controller → CreateUserHandler → Repository write
GET  → Controller → ListUserHandler → Repository read
```

Controllers construct command/query inputs and invoke handlers through direct
dependency injection. The command handler coordinates writes and normalizes input;
the query handler reads records. Both inject the same singleton repository, so
writes are visible to subsequent reads. The module registers the repository and
exports its handlers. Add a focused business service when an operation needs
reusable domain logic. MVC keeps its existing `service.rs` layout.

Existing CQRS features are preserved; migrate their handlers and DI registrations
manually to adopt this layout.

Initial resources implement collection GET and create POST. Update, delete,
get-by-ID, pagination, and their handlers are application extensions. CQRS does
not require separate databases, event sourcing, events, or a message bus; these
are not generated automatically.

## Keep learning

[Providers and modules](skills/xecute/references/architecture/modules.md). Return to the [learning path](skills/xecute/references/index.md) whenever you need a different topic.

---

# Providers and modules

Documentation route: /docs/architecture/modules

Learn how Xecute creates dependencies and shares them between features. First understand the controller → service → repository flow; then read registration, imports, and exports below.

Use `#[derive(Injectable)]` for named-field structs. Dependency fields are resolved
from the container; use `Arc<T>` to share a registered provider. Initialize local
state with `#[inject(default)]` rather than registering that state as a provider:

```rust
use std::sync::Arc;
use tokio::sync::RwLock;
use xecute::Injectable;

#[derive(Injectable)]
pub struct UserRepository {
    #[inject(default)]
    names: RwLock<Vec<String>>,
}

#[derive(Injectable)]
pub struct UserService {
    repository: Arc<UserRepository>,
}
```

The `#[injectable]` struct attribute is also supported. Modules define provider
registrations, imports, and exports:

```rust
use xecute::module;
use super::{UserController, UserService};
use super::repository::UserRepository;

#[module(
    providers = [UserRepository, UserService, UserController],
    controllers = [UserController],
    exports = [UserService],
)]
pub struct UserModule;
```

Register controllers in `providers`; the `controllers` list does not replace
provider registration. Module metadata alone does not mount HTTP routes. The
resource generator also registers module definitions and controller routers in
`AppModule`. For manual assembly, pass all module definitions to
`ModuleGraph::new(...).build()`, resolve controllers, and merge their routers.

Import an owning module to use its exported providers from another module.
Startup validation detects missing registrations, duplicates, circular
relationships, invalid imports/exports, and inaccessible private providers.

For a small manually assembled container:

```rust
let container = xecute::Container::builder()
    .injectable::<UserRepository>()
    .injectable::<UserService>()
    .build()?;
let service = container.resolve::<UserService>()?;
```

| Scope | Behavior |
| --- | --- |
| `singleton` | Default; one instance for the container lifetime |
| `transient` | A new instance for each resolution |
| `request` | Reused within one HTTP request or an explicit request container |

Select a lifecycle with `#[scope("transient")]` or `#[scope("request")]` below
`#[derive(Injectable)]`. Singleton-to-request dependencies are rejected, including
transitive relationships. Generated routing creates request contexts automatically;
explicit `container.request()` contexts are available for jobs and tests.

## Keep learning

[Feature folders](skills/xecute/references/architecture/feature-folders.md). Return to the [learning path](skills/xecute/references/index.md) whenever you need a different topic.

---

# Feature folders

Documentation route: /docs/architecture/feature-folders

Keep one feature’s request types, records, storage, and tests together. Use this guide when your feature starts growing beyond its controller.

All newly generated resources and standalone modules, controllers, and services
live under `src/modules/<feature>/`. Each resource keeps its controller, DI module,
DTOs, entities, repository, and HTTP tests together. CQRS resources also contain
commands and queries. `src/modules/mod.rs` declares each feature;
`AppModule` imports and mounts it through `crate::modules::<feature>`.

```text
src/
├── app_module.rs
├── modules/
│   ├── mod.rs
│   └── user/
│       ├── mod.rs
│       ├── module.rs
│       ├── controller.rs
│       ├── commands/
│       ├── queries/
│       ├── dto/
│       ├── entity/
│       ├── repository/
│       └── tests/
│           ├── mod.rs
│           └── http.rs
└── tests/                 # Shared server/infrastructure tests
```

MVC resources use `service.rs` inside their feature folder instead of CQRS
commands/queries/services directories. This layout is available starting with
CLI 0.1.9; existing root-level features are preserved rather than moved.

## Keep learning

[Provider scopes](skills/xecute/references/architecture/scopes.md). Return to the [learning path](skills/xecute/references/index.md) whenever you need a different topic.

---

# Provider scopes

Documentation route: /docs/architecture/scopes

Choose how long an injected provider lives. Start with the generated singleton behavior; use request or transient scopes only when your application needs a different lifetime.

| Scope | Lifetime |
| --- | --- |
| Singleton (default) | One instance per application container, shared across requests |
| Request | One instance per request context, shared across nested dependencies |
| Transient | A new instance on every resolution |

```rust
use std::sync::Arc;
use xecute::{Injectable, controller, routes};

#[derive(Injectable)]
#[scope("request")]
struct RequestContext {
    #[inject(default)]
    state: std::sync::Mutex<Vec<String>>,
}

#[controller("/example-scope")]
#[derive(Injectable)]
#[scope("request")]
struct ExampleController {
    context: Arc<RequestContext>,
}

#[routes]
impl ExampleController {
    #[get("")]
    async fn get(&self) -> &'static str {
        let _ = &self.context;
        "request scope is active"
    }
}
```

Register both types in a module's providers. Generated `AppModule` uses
`Controller::scoped_router(container.clone())`, creating a request context before
controller middleware and extractors. Nested factories resolve against that same
context. Use a named parameter `context: xecute::Inject<RequestContext>` in a
controller method, or `Inject<T>` in a plain Axum handler, to resolve explicitly.
Plain routers need `xecute::with_container(router, Arc<Container>)`.
To resolve providers in app-level middleware, wrap the fully assembled middleware
pipeline with `with_container` as well. Matching nested boundaries reuse the same
request cache; mixing different container registries in one boundary returns a
safe 500 instead of resolving from the wrong application.
`Controller::router(Arc<Controller>)` remains available for explicitly supplied
controller instances; it cannot recreate their captured dependencies per request.

Use `container.request()` for jobs or tests requiring an explicit scope. Its
clones share a request cache; a second call creates an independent cache. Request
cache ownership is released at completion/cancellation, but any Arc retained by
application code keeps its value alive. `RequestContainer<'a>` remains a
compatibility alias for the owned `RequestScope`.

Startup rejects missing required registrations, duplicate providers/modules,
cycles, private module dependencies, and singleton-to-request dependencies even
through transient providers. Optional providers may be absent, but failures
constructing a registered optional provider propagate. Factories must declare
all dependencies; undeclared resolutions fail instead of risking recursive cache
deadlocks. Custom definitions can mark a declared dependency optional with
`.optional_dependency::<T>()`.

Concurrent resolutions initialize each singleton/request provider once. Factory
errors are cached for that scope; recover external connectivity inside a shared
client instead of expecting factory retries. `container.initialize()` eagerly
constructs singletons and is called before generated applications listen.
Factories are synchronous: initialize asynchronous SDK/database clients at
startup and register their handles as values. A transient injected into a
singleton is created when that singleton is built, then retained by it.

## Keep learning

[Async startup and shutdown](skills/xecute/references/architecture/lifecycle.md). Return to the [learning path](skills/xecute/references/index.md) whenever you need a different topic.

---

# Async startup and shutdown

Documentation route: /docs/architecture/lifecycle

Use lifecycle hooks when resources must connect before requests start and close after work drains. Follow the async startup path below; attribute markers alone do not execute hooks.

Register asynchronous resources with `ProviderDefinition::singleton_async`, then
await `container.initialize_async()` before binding or serving HTTP. Factories
receive an owned `Container`, so they can await connection setup and resolve
**declared** dependencies after await points. Dependencies and their startup hooks
finish before dependent factories run. Existing synchronous factories and derived
providers can depend on these initialized resources without changing their APIs.

```rust
use xecute::{Container, InjectError, ProviderDefinition};

struct Connection;
impl Connection {
    async fn connect() -> Result<Self, InjectError> { Ok(Self) }
    async fn close(&self) -> Result<(), InjectError> { Ok(()) }
}

async fn example() -> Result<(), InjectError> {
let container = Container::builder()
    .provider(
        ProviderDefinition::singleton_async::<Connection, _, _>(vec![], |_| async {
            Connection::connect().await
        })
        .on_init::<Connection, _, _>(|connection| async move {
            // Optional readiness checks or resource warm-up.
            let _ = connection;
            Ok(())
        })
        .on_shutdown::<Connection, _, _>(|connection| async move {
            connection.close().await
        }),
    )
    .build()?;

container.initialize_async().await?;
let connection = container.resolve::<Connection>()?;
// Serve requests, then stop accepting work and drain outstanding requests.
container.shutdown_async().await?;
let _ = connection;
Ok(())
}
```

Use `.on_init::<YourType, _, _>(...)` and `.on_shutdown::<YourType, _, _>(...)`
on a synchronous provider definition as well, including `YourType::definition()`.
The hook type must match the registered provider type. Hooks are singleton-only;
request and transient factories keep their existing resolution behavior. Sync
`initialize()` reports `AsyncInitializationRequired` when async factories or
hooks need startup. It remains usable after async startup completes.

Clones share lifecycle state. Concurrent initialization runs factories and hooks
once; shutdown runs cleanup in reverse dependency order. Startup failures clean
up already constructed resources, including a resource whose init hook failed,
then return and cache the original startup error. Cleanup continues if a hook
returns an error; explicit shutdown returns the first cleanup error. A factory
that fails before returning owns cleanup of its partially constructed resources.

Shutdown is explicit: dropping a container does not execute async hooks. After
startup cancellation, call `shutdown_async()` to clean constructed resources;
startup cannot be retried on that container. Cancelled shutdown can be resumed,
but the interrupted hook is not retried. Keep cleanup hooks bounded and avoid
cancelling them when possible. Hooks and factories must not call lifecycle
methods recursively on the same container. Existing `Arc` references remain
accessible after cleanup; finish application work before shutting down.

For module-based applications, attach definitions with
`ModuleDefinition::provider(...)`, then build with `ModuleGraph` as usual.
For generated applications using async resources, build the container from
`AppModule::definitions()` and await initialization before calling
`AppModule::router_with_container(container.clone())`; the synchronous
`AppModule::container()` helper cannot initialize async resources. Retain a
container clone for cleanup after graceful request draining, including startup
errors after initialization (for example, a failed listener bind).

With the `testing` feature, use `TestingModule::compile_async().await` and call
`shutdown_async()` when the test finishes. Provider overrides replace factories
and hooks together. Existing lifecycle attribute markers such as
`#[on_module_init]` remain placeholders; use the executable registration methods
above.

Run `cargo run -p xecute --example async_lifecycle` for a complete example with
async connection setup, a synchronous dependent service, and explicit cleanup.

[Choose your next guide](skills/xecute/references/index.md). Return to the [learning path](skills/xecute/references/index.md) whenever you need a different topic.

# Controllers and extractors

Documentation route: /docs/http/controllers

A controller connects an HTTP request to an application operation. Use the example below inside a generated user feature, then choose body, path, or query inputs from the extractor table.

Use `#[controller]` on the struct and `#[routes]` on its inherent impl. An MVC
resource controller can use the generated service and DTO as follows:

```rust
//! HTTP endpoints for the user feature.

use std::sync::Arc;
use xecute::prelude::*;
use super::{dto::CreateUserDto, entity::User, service::UserService};

#[controller("/user")]
#[derive(Injectable)]
/// User collection and creation endpoints.
pub struct UserController {
    service: Arc<UserService>,
}

#[routes]
impl UserController {
    #[get("")]
    #[api(summary = "List users", tag = "Users", operation_id = "listUsers")]
    #[resp(200, "Current users", json = Vec<User>)]
    async fn list(&self) -> Json<Vec<User>> {
        Json(self.service.list().await)
    }

    #[post("")]
    #[body(json = CreateUserDto)]
    #[resp(201, "User created", json = User)]
    #[resp(422, "Invalid payload")]
    #[resp(503, "Repository capacity exhausted")]
    async fn create(
        &self,
        #[body] payload: CreateUserDto,
    ) -> Result<(HttpStatus, Json<User>), HttpError> {
        let user = self.service.create(payload).await
            .map_err(|_| HttpError::new(HttpStatus::SERVICE_UNAVAILABLE))?;
        Ok((HttpStatus::CREATED, Json(user)))
    }
}
```

Supported HTTP annotations are `#[get]`, `#[post]`, `#[put]`, `#[patch]`,
`#[delete]`, `#[head]`, and `#[options]`. A handler has one HTTP annotation.
Prefixes and nonempty route suffixes must start with `/`.

| Parameter | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `#[body] payload: CreateUserDto` | Decode JSON and validate the DTO |
| `#[query] filter: SearchDto` | Decode the query string and validate the DTO |
| `#[param] id: String` | Extract an Axum path parameter, e.g. `#[get("/{id}")]` |
| `identity: axum::Extension<Identity>` | Use an Axum extractor directly |

Receiver handlers use `&self`, simple parameter names, and async, non-generic
methods. Only one JSON body parameter is supported. When using ordinary Axum
extractors, place any body-consuming extractor last. `#[body]` is moved to the
last extractor position automatically.

`Controller::router(Arc<Controller>)` builds its Axum router.
`Controller::api_operations()` returns documentation metadata. The older
`#[controller("/prefix")] impl Controller` syntax remains supported.

## Keep learning

[DTO validation](skills/xecute/references/http/validation.md). Return to the [learning path](skills/xecute/references/index.md) whenever you need a different topic.

---

# DTO validation

Documentation route: /docs/http/validation

Put request rules in DTO structs under dto/mod.rs. Read the example, then use the status table to understand which requests are rejected before your handler runs.

Validation uses the `validator` crate directly. Generated request DTOs derive
`Deserialize`, `Validate`, and `JsonSchema`, and reject unknown fields:

```rust
//! User request contracts and validation rules.

use schemars::JsonSchema;
use serde::Deserialize;
use validator::{Validate, ValidationError};

#[derive(Deserialize, Validate, JsonSchema)]
#[serde(deny_unknown_fields)]
/// Validated input for user creation.
pub struct CreateUserDto {
    /// Display name containing 3–100 characters and non-whitespace content.
    #[schemars(length(min = 3, max = 100))]
    #[validate(length(min = 3, max = 100), custom(function = "non_blank"))]
    pub name: String,
}

fn non_blank(value: &str) -> Result<(), ValidationError> {
    if value.trim().is_empty() {
        return Err(ValidationError::new("name must not be blank"));
    }
    Ok(())
}
```

`#[body]` and `#[query]` run validation at the controller's extraction boundary.
You do not call `.validate()` manually in the controller. Invalid input returns
an HTTP response before the controller method, service, command handler, or
repository runs. Middleware already entered can still process that response.
Direct calls to services or command handlers bypass HTTP extraction; enforce any
required domain invariants at those entry points too.

| Input failure | HTTP status |
| --- | --- |
| Malformed JSON syntax | `400 Bad Request` |
| Missing JSON fields, wrong field types, unknown fields, failed DTO rules | `422 Unprocessable Entity` |
| Missing/unsupported JSON content type | `415 Unsupported Media Type` |
| Query decoding failure | `400 Bad Request` |
| Query DTO validation failure | `422 Unprocessable Entity` |
| Oversized request body | `413 Payload Too Large` |

The generated server normalizes failures to a safe JSON envelope:

```json
{
  "error": {
    "code": "validation_failed",
    "message": "Invalid request data",
    "request_id": "<request UUID>"
  }
}
```

Responses include `X-Request-Id`. Public validation errors do not expose submitted
values or field-level validation details. Use explicit domain-error mappings to
`HttpError` for safe application messages. The runtime produces JSON errors; the
generated middleware supplies correlation IDs and normalizes other failures.

## Keep learning

[Middleware](skills/xecute/references/http/middleware.md). Return to the [learning path](skills/xecute/references/index.md) whenever you need a different topic.

# Middleware

Documentation route: /docs/http/middleware

Middleware wraps requests and responses around a handler. Use it for shared HTTP behavior; follow the execution order below before combining application, controller, and route middleware.

This section requires runtime/macros 0.1.5 or later; see [release status](#release-status).

Middleware functions accept `Request` and `Next` from `xecute::middleware` and
return a response or another `IntoResponse` value. Call `next.run(request).await`
to continue. Return directly to stop further middleware, validation, and handler
execution.

## App-level middleware

The generator creates `src/middleware.rs`. Replace its default configuration
with a middleware registration, for example:

```rust
use xecute::{Application, middleware::{Request, Next, Response}};

pub fn configure(app: Application) -> Application {
    app.use_middleware(audit)
}

pub async fn audit(request: Request, next: Next) -> Response {
    let mut response = next.run(request).await;
    response.headers_mut().insert("x-audited", "true".parse().unwrap());
    response
}
```

The generated server invokes this hook for application routes, documentation,
health probes, and unmatched URLs. Request logging and response normalization
wrap the hook, including its early error responses. A global authentication
policy must explicitly allow any public endpoints it needs, such as probes.

Existing projects can wrap their assembled router directly:

```rust
let app = xecute::Application::new(router)
    .use_middleware(audit)
    .use_middleware(metrics)
    .into_router();
```

Add routes before constructing/finalizing this pipeline. Only routes and
fallbacks already present are wrapped. Global registrations can be closures
capturing shared state such as `Arc<YourDependency>`.

## Controller-level middleware

Place middleware below the controller attribute:

```rust
#[controller("/user")]
#[middleware(crate::middleware::audit)]
#[derive(Injectable)]
/// User collection and creation endpoints.
pub struct UserController {
    service: Arc<UserService>,
}
```

It runs for every matched route belonging to that controller. It does not run
for unrelated URLs that return 404.

Controller middleware can also be declared on the routing impl:

```rust
#[routes]
#[middleware(crate::middleware::audit)]
impl UserController {
    // HTTP handlers...
}
```

If the controller has both struct and impl middleware, struct middleware wraps
impl middleware. Use the standard `#[controller]` struct plus `#[routes]` impl
form when combining controller metadata and middleware.

## Route-level middleware

Place middleware on a handler inside a `#[routes]` impl:

```rust
#[routes]
impl UserController {
    #[get("")]
    #[middleware(crate::middleware::audit)]
    async fn list(&self) -> Json<Vec<User>> {
        Json(self.service.list().await)
    }
}
```

This middleware applies only to that HTTP method and route. It does not attach
to a POST handler sharing the same path.

An early-return middleware can reject a request without invoking the controller:

```rust
use xecute::middleware::{Request, Next};

async fn temporarily_unavailable(_: Request, _: Next) -> axum::http::StatusCode {
    axum::http::StatusCode::SERVICE_UNAVAILABLE
}
```

## Execution order

```text
Request:
  App middleware → Controller struct middleware → Controller impl middleware
  → Route middleware → Extraction/validation → Handler

Response:
  Handler/rejection → Route → Controller impl → Controller struct → App
```

Within a scope, declaration order is execution order:

```rust
#[middleware(first, second)]
// Equivalent ordering to consecutive #[middleware(first)] and #[middleware(second)].
```

The response unwinds in reverse order. A short-circuit skips later middleware
and the handler; earlier middleware can still inspect or modify its response.

Keep `#[controller]` and `#[routes]` above their middleware annotations so the
owning macros process them. Empty middleware lists and middleware on methods
without an HTTP route attribute are rejected. Controller/route annotations take
function paths; use app-level closures or request extensions for shared state.
These are HTTP middleware, not automatic CQRS handler pipelines.

[Swagger and OpenAPI](skills/xecute/references/http/openapi.md). Return to the [learning path](skills/xecute/references/index.md) whenever you need a different topic.

# Swagger and OpenAPI

Documentation route: /docs/http/openapi

Use Swagger to try endpoints and OpenAPI to describe their contract. Start with the generated /docs/ endpoint, then add metadata when you add routes or change DTOs.

Every generated project includes embedded Swagger UI at `/docs/` and an OpenAPI
3.1 document at `/docs/openapi.json`. Resource generation adds each controller's
operations automatically. Set `docs.enabled = false` in `config/AppConfig.toml` to disable both routes.

| Annotation | Purpose |
| --- | --- |
| `#[api(summary = "...", tag = "...", operation_id = "...")]` | Describe an endpoint and its operation ID |
| `#[body(json = RequestDto)]` | Declare the JSON body type; it must match the `#[body]` parameter |
| `#[resp(201, "Created", json = ResponseDto)]` | Describe a response and schema |
| `#[resp(422, "Invalid payload")]` | Describe a response without a JSON schema |

DTOs and response entities derive `schemars::JsonSchema`. Keep schema constraints
such as `#[schemars(length(...))]` aligned with validation attributes. Schema
generation describes data; it does not itself validate requests. API metadata
does not change the HTTP status returned by a handler.

For manual documentation assembly, use `Controller::api_operations()` with
`xecute::openapi_document(title, version, operations)`.

## Keep learning

[Errors and domain mappings](skills/xecute/references/http/errors.md). Return to the [learning path](skills/xecute/references/index.md) whenever you need a different topic.

---

# Errors and domain mappings

Documentation route: /docs/http/errors

Turn application failures into safe HTTP responses. Choose a status and public message deliberately; keep internal errors out of the response.

Handlers and services can return typed domain errors. Map expected failures
explicitly using `From<DomainError> for HttpError`; controllers returning
`Result<T, HttpError>` can then use `?`.

```rust
use xecute::{HttpError, HttpStatus};

struct EmailTaken;
impl From<EmailTaken> for HttpError {
    fn from(_: EmailTaken) -> Self {
        HttpError::public(
            HttpStatus::CONFLICT,
            "email_taken",
            "Email is already registered",
        )
    }
}
```

The response contains `error.code`, `error.message`, and a server-generated
`error.request_id` matching `X-Request-Id`. Custom mappings survive generated
response normalization. Public custom messages and codes are static API text;
never include user input or secrets. Codes accept lowercase ASCII letters,
digits, and underscores, up to 64 characters. Invalid codes use default details.
All 5xx errors use safe default messages even if custom text is supplied. Invalid
success statuses passed to `HttpError::new` become 500. Log an underlying failure
explicitly before mapping it; Xecute does not serialize error Display text.

`HttpError` produces a JSON envelope on its own, with an empty request ID when
there is no request boundary. Generated applications already normalize errors,
preserve protocol/CORS/retry headers, discard stale representation headers, and
attach IDs. For a plain Axum router, install
`xecute::exceptions::exception_boundary(router)` once after assembling routes.
This helper normalizes error responses; generated servers also have their
existing panic-catching and deadline middleware. A panic in an independent
background task is outside the HTTP boundary.

## Keep learning

[API version groups](skills/xecute/references/http/versioning.md). Return to the [learning path](skills/xecute/references/index.md) whenever you need a different topic.

# API version groups

Documentation route: /docs/http/versioning

Use explicit version groups when clients need different API contracts at the same time. Each group can have its own routes and API document.

Generated applications register only v1 in
`src/server/versions.rs`:

| URL | Contract |
| --- | --- |
| `/example` | Existing unversioned resource alias |
| `/v1/example` | Version-one resources, using the same v1 service/container |
| `/docs/v1/` | Version-one Swagger UI |
| `/docs/v1/openapi.json` | Version-one contract, with `/v1/...` paths |

`/docs/` and `/docs/openapi.json` continue to describe the unversioned aliases.
No v2 module, routes, or documentation are generated. Additional version groups
can be registered explicitly using the runtime API when needed.

```rust
use xecute::{ApiVersion, ApiVersions};

let versions = ApiVersions::new()
    .with(ApiVersion::new("v1", v1_router, V1Controller::api_operations())?)?;
let router = versions.mount(axum::Router::new());
let documents = versions.documents("My API")?;
```

Supply controller paths relative to the group; the router and documented paths
receive the same prefix. Canonical labels are `v1`, `v2`, etc, with positive u32
version numbers. Invalid labels, duplicate groups, and conflicting contracts fail
before serving. The same operation ID/schema name may appear in different
version documents. Global application policies wrap all groups.

```toml
[api]
versioning_enabled = true

[docs]
enabled = true
```

Set `api.versioning_enabled = false` to keep only unversioned aliases. Set
`docs.enabled = false` to hide all Swagger/OpenAPI routes while keeping API routes
active. `GET /` lists each enabled version's Swagger and OpenAPI paths.
The registration pattern is explicit URL versioning; header-based versioning and
automatic deprecation/sunset behavior are not implied.

## Keep learning

[Multipart uploads](skills/xecute/references/http/uploads.md). Return to the [learning path](skills/xecute/references/index.md) whenever you need a different topic.

# Multipart uploads

Documentation route: /docs/http/uploads

Use this guide for multipart file requests. It needs the upload feature and explicit storage configuration; ordinary JSON endpoints do not need it.

A runnable controller example is included at
[`xecute/examples/file_upload.rs`](https://github.com/morshedulmunna/xecute/blob/main/xecute/examples/file_upload.rs).
Run from the repository root:

```sh
cargo run -p xecute --example file_upload --features upload
curl -F 'file=@report.pdf;type=application/pdf' http://127.0.0.1:3000/uploads
curl -F 'file=@photo.png;type=image/png' -F 'file=@report.pdf;type=application/pdf' \
  http://127.0.0.1:3000/uploads
```

The controller returns HTTP 201 with an array of `key`, `original_name`,
`content_type`, `size`, and `sha256`. It accepts PNG/JPEG/PDF content, at most four
files, 1 MiB per file, and 2 MiB total; HTTP framing has an additional 64 KiB
allowance. MIME signatures must match declared types. Files are private under
`target/file-upload-example/objects/`, with temporary files in `staging/`.
`/openapi.json` describes the multipart endpoint; the example has no download route.
Invalid multipart requests return 400, oversized uploads 413, invalid types 415,
and missing/empty/excess files 422, with a consistent error envelope and request ID.

This standalone example binds loopback and is separate from generated projects.
Before deploying it, add authentication and application rate/time limits, use a
persistent private storage directory, and define cleanup/retention. Content
signature validation is not malware scanning. Batch rollback is best effort;
crashes or cancellation can leave objects requiring reconciliation.


New projects do not include a built-in uploads module or upload configuration.
To implement uploads in your own feature module, enable the runtime `upload`
feature (and `upload-s3` for S3). The runtime provides `UploadPolicy`,
`UploadService`, `LocalStorage`, `UploadStorage`, and optional `S3Storage`.
Use `#[multipart]` on the upload handler for multipart OpenAPI metadata.

```toml
[dependencies]
xecute = { version = "0.1.8", features = ["upload"] }
```

Apply HTTP body limits and authentication to your own upload route, keep storage
outside `public/`, and configure its policy and backend explicitly.

[Static files](skills/xecute/references/http/static-files.md). Return to the [learning path](skills/xecute/references/index.md) whenever you need a different topic.

# Static files

Documentation route: /docs/http/static-files

Serve files that are intentionally public. Start with the generated public directory and /static/ prefix, then review path and fallback behavior before changing them.

Newly generated applications include `public/index.html`, served at `/static` and
`/static/`, plus `public/hello.txt`, served at
`http://127.0.0.1:3000/static/hello.txt`. Static serving is enabled by default,
without environment settings. Add files to `public/` and access them at `/static/<filename>`.
For example, `public/images/logo.png` is served at `/static/images/logo.png`.
To customize the directory, prefix, or enabled state, edit `StaticConfig` in
`src/configs/static_files.rs`. Relative directories use the application's working
directory; the public directory must exist and cannot be the application root or a symlink.

Files support GET, HEAD, MIME types, conditional requests, and byte ranges through
Tower HTTP `ServeDir`. Directory listings and nested directory indexes are disabled. The mount root
serves `public/index.html`; other assets use explicit filenames. Hidden path components, parent traversal, and
symlinked assets are rejected. Keep public directories limited to intended public
assets; static files share the application's CORS, request IDs, security headers,
logging, rate limits, and global middleware. HTML retains the restrictive API CSP;
this is asset serving, not a generated SPA hosting configuration.

The Docker image copies `public/` into the runtime image. For another static directory,
adapt the Dockerfile or mount the asset directory read-only. Change files in the
public directory directly or mount updated assets; there is no binary embedding.

[Choose your next guide](skills/xecute/references/index.md). Return to the [learning path](skills/xecute/references/index.md) whenever you need a different topic.

# Application configuration

Documentation route: /docs/configuration/application

Start here to change generated server settings. Edit config/AppConfig.toml for application settings and use environment variables for secrets.

Ordinary settings live in the generated `config/AppConfig.toml`. Commit this file;
keep credentials in `.env` or inject them through your deployment's secret store.
`.env` is optional and ignored by Git/Docker. Process variables take precedence
over `.env` for secrets. Ordinary settings have no environment fallback or override.

```toml
[server]
bind_address = "127.0.0.1:3000"
request_timeout_seconds = 30
shutdown_grace_seconds = 10
body_limit_bytes = 1048576
max_in_flight_requests = 256

[rate_limit]
requests = 60
window_seconds = 60
max_clients = 10000

[cors]
origins = ["https://example.com", "http://localhost:5173"]
allowed_methods = ["GET", "POST"]
allowed_headers = ["content-type", "authorization"]
exposed_headers = ["x-request-id", "retry-after"]
allow_credentials = false
max_age_seconds = 600

[docs]
enabled = true

[logging]
filter = "info"
stdout_enabled = true
file_dir = "logs"
```

The generated CORS origin list is empty by default. Origins must be exact HTTP(S)
origins without paths, credentials, wildcards, or trailing slashes. Credentials
require a nonempty origin list. Arrays are native TOML arrays, without JSON or
dotenv quoting. Invalid types, unknown keys, invalid protocol values, and numeric
bounds fail startup before logging/listening. Missing individual values use typed
defaults, but the file itself must exist. Request limits must be positive; the
CORS cache duration may be zero.

`Config::from_file()` reads `config/AppConfig.toml` relative to the working directory.
`Config::from_path(path)` supports an explicit file chosen in bootstrap code.
The file is parsed once into a validated snapshot shared with logger startup;
there is no automatic production reload. Development hot reload watches TOML
files and restarts the process when settings change.

The Dockerfile includes this file and adapts only the generated loopback bind to
`0.0.0.0:3000`. Custom bind addresses remain unchanged. To supply deployment
settings, mount a replacement `/app/config/AppConfig.toml` read-only. The default private
`/app/logs` directory is owned by UID 65532; custom log mounts must also be writable
by this user. A read-only root filesystem requires writable log storage or an
empty `logging.file_dir`.

For custom settings, use `xecute::config::ConfigFile` with dotted paths and extend
the allowed-key schema in `src/configs/server.rs`. Use `Env::process().secret(key)`
for required credentials and tokens. The template `.env.example` contains only
commented credential examples, with no active configuration or fake secrets.

## Keep learning

[Typed configuration](skills/xecute/references/configuration/typed.md). Return to the [learning path](skills/xecute/references/index.md) whenever you need a different topic.
