# Typed configuration

Documentation route: /docs/configuration/typed

Use typed configuration when your own feature needs validated settings. Define a Rust type and read it at startup rather than parsing environment values inside every handler.

These APIs are available with CLI 0.1.13, runtime 0.1.8, and macros 0.1.6.
Update the CLI before generating a new project. Existing applications require
corresponding dependency and source changes; updating the CLI does not rewrite them.

The common configuration boundary separates `ConfigFile` for ordinary settings
from `Env` for secrets. Both report value-redacted validation errors. TOML parsing
preserves native types: `false` is a boolean, while `"false"` is an invalid type
for a boolean setting. `get_or` defaults only absent keys; supplied bad values
remain errors. `range` enforces numeric bounds; `required` rejects missing keys.
Generated configuration rejects unknown keys so typos cannot silently disable policies.

```rust
use xecute::config::{ConfigError, ConfigFile, Env, SecretString};

struct DatabaseConfig {
    url: SecretString,
    pool_size: u64,
}
impl DatabaseConfig {
    fn load(file: &ConfigFile) -> Result<Self, ConfigError> {
        Ok(Self {
            url: Env::process().secret("DATABASE_URL")?,
            pool_size: file.range("database.pool_size", 10, 1, 100)?,
        })
    }
}
```

Add `database.pool_size` to the generated allowed-key schema when introducing
this custom setting. Initialize custom configuration before binding the listener.
`SecretString` redacts Debug output and requires `.expose()` for SDK/client access;
it does not promise memory zeroization. `.env` and TOML parse errors omit source
contents. Tests can use `ConfigFile::parse(source)` and map-backed `Env::new`
without changing process variables. Configuration is a startup snapshot.

## Keep learning

[Logging and exporters](skills/xecute/references/configuration/logging.md). Return to the [learning path](skills/xecute/references/index.md) whenever you need a different topic.

---

# Logging and exporters

Documentation route: /docs/configuration/logging

Start with console logs, then configure file rotation or an exporter when you need them. This guide shows which logging behavior belongs to your generated application.

Logging outputs use these settings in `config/AppConfig.toml`:

```toml
[logging]
stdout_enabled = true
file_dir = "logs"
```

`logging.stdout_enabled` controls JSON console output. A nonempty `logging.file_dir`
enables JSON file output and creates the private directory. Remove it or leave it
empty to disable file output. Generated projects include both settings above.
`logging.filter` continues to filter events across all outputs.

Files use the `app` prefix, daily rotation, and retention of seven matching files.
These defaults live in `src/configs/logging.rs` and can be changed in code.
Setting stdout false and omitting the file directory allows an exporter-only
configuration. An unwritable enabled file destination fails startup.

The file sink uses a dedicated writer thread and an 8192-entry bounded queue.
A full queue applies backpressure rather than silently dropping events. The
`LoggerGuard` returned from initialization is retained in `server/bootstrap.rs`
until normal server shutdown so pending writes are flushed. Forced termination
cannot guarantee pending log delivery. Built-in request events continue to omit
payloads, cookies, authorization headers, and query strings.

The default `/logs/` path is ignored by Git and Docker. Configured log storage
must remain outside the public static directory, even if file output is currently
disabled. For a read-only container with file output enabled, mount private log
storage writable by the application's UID 65532. Console logging can instead be
collected by the deployment's log collector.

## Sentry, Grafana/Loki, OpenTelemetry, and custom exporters

Application modules emit standard `tracing` events, so business code does not need
to change when a new destination is added:

```rust
tracing::info!(operation = "create_user", "User created");
tracing::warn!(operation = "create_user", "Capacity reached");
```

`src/server/logging.rs` exposes `init_with_layer(&config, exporter_layer)` for a
`tracing_subscriber::Layer<Registry>`. Replace the default bootstrap initialization
with this call after configuring your chosen SDK/collector. Standard console
and file sinks remain independently configurable and continue to receive the
same events. A test exporter verifies that file logging and an extra layer can
receive an event together.

For a future Sentry or OpenTelemetry integration, add its SDK dependencies and
initialize its layer/provider before installing the subscriber. Keep SDK guards
alive for the server lifetime and shut exporters down according to that SDK's
requirements. Grafana/Loki deployments can also ingest the existing JSON stdout
or files through a log collector. No cloud SDK, credentials, or outbound exporter
is configured by default. Per-backend transport/retries/authentication belong in
the selected SDK or collector, not in controllers or services.

Static serving, shared environment access, and configurable file/exporter logging
are available starting with CLI 0.1.11. Existing applications need the corresponding source
and dependency updates; updating the CLI does not rewrite an existing app.

## Shared configuration readers

`src/configs/environment.rs` re-exports the shared runtime readers.
`configs::load_env()` loads optional credentials once; `Env::process()` and
`configs::read_env(key)` read secrets with process-over-dotenv precedence.
Ordinary settings use `ConfigFile::load("config/AppConfig.toml")` and typed dotted paths.
Generated server and logger use the same validated configuration snapshot.

```rust
let token = xecute::config::Env::process().secret("API_TOKEN")?;
let file = xecute::config::ConfigFile::load("config/AppConfig.toml")?;
let timeout = file.range("server.request_timeout_seconds", 30, 1, 3600)?;
```

[Server defaults](skills/xecute/references/configuration/server-defaults.md). Return to the [learning path](skills/xecute/references/index.md) whenever you need a different topic.

# Server defaults

Documentation route: /docs/configuration/server-defaults

Understand the policies your generated server already applies, including limits and health endpoints. Review this page before changing middleware or deploying.

Generated applications include the following HTTP policies:

| Policy | Default behavior |
| --- | --- |
| Logging | One flat JSON completion log per request, filtered by `logging.filter` |
| Correlation | UUID `X-Request-Id` response header |
| Rate limit | 60 requests per socket peer IP per 60-second fixed window |
| Limiter capacity | At most 10,000 tracked IPs per process |
| Concurrency | At most 256 active handlers; overload returns `503` |
| Deadline | 30 seconds until response headers; expiry returns `504` |
| Body limit | 1 MiB; oversized declared or consumed bodies return `413` |
| CORS | No allowed cross-origin browser origins by default |
| Response headers | `nosniff`, frame denial, no-referrer, restrictive API CSP |
| Errors | Safe JSON envelopes for rejection and failure responses |
| Shutdown | Ctrl-C/SIGTERM handling with a 10-second drain deadline |
| Health | Liveness and startup-readiness probes bypass built-in quotas/concurrency limits |

Logs omit payloads, authorization headers, cookies, query strings, and full URLs.
Matched requests log the route template; unmatched requests may log the requested
path. Streaming-body completion is not included in latency measurements.

The timeout and concurrency boundary ends when response headers are produced.
Timeouts cancel the handler future but cannot undo completed writes or stop
separately spawned tasks. Readiness indicates startup success until you add
checks for databases and other dependencies.

## Keep learning

[Welcome and startup URLs](skills/xecute/references/configuration/welcome.md). Return to the [learning path](skills/xecute/references/index.md) whenever you need a different topic.

# Welcome and startup URLs

Documentation route: /docs/configuration/welcome

Use the welcome response and startup output to find your application’s enabled URLs. Only configured routes and documents appear.

`GET /` returns HTTP 200 with the application name, `status: "ok"`, a welcome
message, and `documentation: "/docs/"`. With `docs.enabled = false` in `config/AppConfig.toml`, the
`documentation` field is null. Other unregistered paths still return the normal
404 envelope. The root route is defined in `src/server/router.rs` and can be
customized there.

Startup emits one `server listening` JSON log with the actual bound address and
local URL, including when binding port zero. `GET /` exposes the address, URL,
Swagger and OpenAPI paths, versioned documentation links, and static-file mount.
Disabled endpoints are null or omitted from the version list. Wildcard bindings
use loopback URLs and IPv6 addresses are bracketed. Configure public URLs
separately when running behind a TLS ingress or reverse proxy.

Available starting with CLI 0.1.10. Existing projects need the corresponding
server changes; updating the CLI does not rewrite them. The runtime crate is unchanged.

# PostgreSQL

Documentation route: /docs/integrations/postgres

Replace in-memory storage when records must survive a restart. You need a PostgreSQL server, a connection URL, and the postgres feature; follow configuration, provider registration, then repository examples.

Xecute's optional `postgres` feature integrates SQLx 0.9 with dependency injection
and async application lifecycle. It provides a shared connection pool, validated
configuration, startup migrations, readiness checks, and graceful pool cleanup.
Repositories use native SQLx queries and transactions; Xecute does not add an ORM.

Enable the runtime's `postgres` feature:

```toml
[dependencies]
xecute = { version = "0.1", features = ["postgres"] }
```

`postgres` is disabled by default. You do not need SQLx as a separate dependency:
use `xecute::database::sqlx`. No database URL is needed at compile time because
this integration uses parameterized runtime queries, not schema-checked macros.
MVC and CQRS generators still produce in-memory repositories; database adoption
is explicit and existing generated application files are not rewritten.

## Run the complete example

From the repository root, start a disposable development PostgreSQL instance:

```sh
docker run --detach --rm --name xecute-postgres-demo \
  -e POSTGRES_USER=xecute \
  -e POSTGRES_PASSWORD=xecute_dev_only \
  -e POSTGRES_DB=xecute_demo \
  -p 127.0.0.1:55432:5432 postgres:17

docker exec xecute-postgres-demo pg_isready -U xecute -d xecute_demo

# Wait for pg_isready to report "accepting connections", then:
export DATABASE_URL='postgres://xecute:xecute_dev_only@127.0.0.1:55432/xecute_demo'
cargo run -p xecute --example postgres --features postgres

# Re-running creates another user; existing records remain in the database.
# Remove the disposable container and its database after the demo:
docker stop xecute-postgres-demo
```

The example applies `examples/postgres/migrations/202610270001_create_users.sql`,
creates a user and audit entry in one transaction, reads the user back, and closes
the pool. Its separate `repository.rs` is reusable as a persistence-layer example.
For durable local development, mount a named Docker volume at PostgreSQL's data
directory instead of using this disposable setup.

## Configuration and secrets

Read `DATABASE_URL` from the environment or a secret manager. Do not put it into
ordinary application TOML, source control, log messages, or HTTP error responses.
Xecute does not automatically load `.env`; generated applications already have an
environment loader, while standalone examples use the process environment.

```rust
use std::time::Duration;
use xecute::database::{PostgresConfig, sqlx::postgres::PgSslMode};

let url = std::env::var("DATABASE_URL")?;
let config = PostgresConfig::new(&url)?
    .pool_limits(0, 10)?
    .acquire_timeout(Duration::from_secs(5))?
    .ssl_mode(PgSslMode::VerifyFull);
```

Defaults are zero minimum connections, ten maximum connections, and a five-second
pool acquisition timeout. Maximum must be positive, minimum cannot exceed maximum,
and acquisition timeout must be positive. Acquisition includes establishing a
connection; it is not a SQL statement execution timeout. Configure PostgreSQL
`statement_timeout` separately when needed. Budget pool sizes across all replicas
against your database's connection limit.

TLS uses SQLx's PostgreSQL settings. For production, use `VerifyFull` with a
trusted server certificate and matching hostname; supply an appropriate CA using
SQLx's connection URL options, such as `sslrootcert`. Local Docker PostgreSQL does
not offer TLS by default, so the local example uses the driver's default settings.
SQL statement logging is disabled by this wrapper. `PostgresConfig` debug output
redacts connection options, and `DatabaseError` exposes only static messages.

## Modules, startup, and shutdown

```rust
use std::path::Path;
use xecute::{ModuleDefinition, ModuleGraph};
use xecute::database::{PostgresConfig, PostgresDatabase, sqlx::migrate::Migrator};

async fn setup() -> Result<(), Box<dyn std::error::Error + Send + Sync>> {
    let config = PostgresConfig::new(&std::env::var("DATABASE_URL")?)?;
    let migrations = Migrator::new(Path::new("./migrations")).await?;
    let database_module = ModuleDefinition::new("database")
        .provider(PostgresDatabase::provider_with_migrations(config, migrations))
        .export::<PostgresDatabase>();

    // Add your feature's repository/service/handler definitions to this module.
    let users_module = ModuleDefinition::new("users").import("database");
    let container = ModuleGraph::new(vec![database_module, users_module]).build()?;
    container.initialize_async().await?;
    let work: Result<(), Box<dyn std::error::Error + Send + Sync>> = async {
        let database = container.resolve::<PostgresDatabase>()?;
        database.health_check().await?;
        // Serve traffic, then stop accepting work and drain in-flight requests.
        Ok(())
    }.await;
    let cleanup = container.shutdown_async().await;
    work?;
    cleanup?;
    Ok(())
}
```

Register the database once, export it from its owning module, and import that
module wherever a repository requires it. Repository definitions must declare
`ProviderKey::of::<PostgresDatabase>()` as a dependency. Dependent factories run
only after the pool connects and migrations finish. Failed startup prevents
serving and closes the pool if it was constructed. `PostgresDatabase::provider`
omits migrations when your deployment runs them separately.

Generated applications currently use synchronous `AppModule::container()`. For
async resources, build a `ModuleGraph` from `AppModule::definitions()` instead,
await `initialize_async()`, then pass a retained `Arc<Container>` to
`AppModule::router_with_container(container.clone())`. That routing helper remains
usable after async startup. Ensure the exported database module definition and
importing feature definitions are included in the graph.

Retain the container for cleanup on every exit path after successful startup,
including router construction, listener binding, serving, and graceful-shutdown
errors. Capture application work in an async block returning a `Result`, await
`shutdown_async()` afterward, then return the result; the complete example shows
this pattern. There are no async cleanup hooks in `Drop`. Release checked-out
connections and transactions before closing: pool closure waits for them. If
bounded shutdown is required, apply your application's timeout policy explicitly.

## Migration workflow

Use SQLx migration filenames such as `202610270001_create_users.sql`. Version
numbers must be unique and ordered. Applied migrations are recorded in
`_sqlx_migrations`; re-running validates checksums and applies only pending files.
SQLx's PostgreSQL migration locking serializes concurrent migration runners.
Do not edit an applied migration: add a new version instead.

The example loads migration files at runtime. Deploy the migration directory and
resolve its path explicitly, or run migrations as a deployment step before starting
applications. You can also enable SQLx's `macros` feature in your application to
embed migrations with `sqlx::migrate!`; follow SQLx's build-script guidance so new
SQL files trigger recompilation. Xecute does not enable SQLx macros by default.

Run schema-changing migrations with an appropriately privileged deployment role.
Runtime access can use a separate restricted application role with
`PostgresDatabase::provider`. There is no automatic schema rollback on application
shutdown. Migration SQL is trusted application code; backup and rollback strategy
remain deployment responsibilities.

## Repository and transaction boundaries

Keep the application flow:

```text
MVC:  Controller → Service → Repository → PostgreSQL
CQRS: Controller → Command/Query Handler → Repository → PostgreSQL
```

Bind user input with `$1`, `$2`, and `.bind(value)`. Never interpolate user input
into a SQL string. Methods on the repository return application entities or DTOs;
controllers should not contain SQL.

```rust
use xecute::database::{PostgresDatabase, sqlx};

async fn create_user(db: &PostgresDatabase, name: &str) -> Result<i64, sqlx::Error> {
    let mut tx = db.begin().await?;
    let id = sqlx::query_scalar::<_, i64>(
        "INSERT INTO xecute_example_users (name) VALUES ($1) RETURNING id",
    ).bind(name).fetch_one(&mut *tx).await?;

    sqlx::query(
        "INSERT INTO xecute_example_audit (user_id, action) VALUES ($1, $2)",
    ).bind(id).bind("created").execute(&mut *tx).await?;

    tx.commit().await?;
    Ok(id)
}
```

All participating writes must execute against `&mut *tx`, not `db.pool()`, or they
will not share the transaction. Call `commit()` on success or `rollback()` when
handling an error explicitly. Dropping an uncommitted SQLx transaction schedules
rollback. Avoid holding a transaction across unrelated network calls.

For a use case spanning multiple repositories, the handler/service should own the
transaction and pass `&mut PgConnection` (obtained via `&mut *tx`) to each repository
method. Starting a new transaction inside every repository cannot make multiple
repositories' writes atomic. Automatic transaction propagation, distributed
transactions, and automatic retries are not provided.

## Readiness and error handling

Use `health_check().await` in a readiness endpoint and return HTTP 503 when the
database is unavailable. Keep liveness independent of PostgreSQL connectivity.
The generated readiness route is not changed automatically.

`DatabaseError` redacts configuration, connection, migration, and readiness errors.
Lifecycle registration maps setup failures to static `InjectError` messages.
`begin()` and native SQLx repository queries retain SQLx errors for application
handling, including SQLSTATE codes for unique/foreign-key violations. Map these
to domain errors and safe HTTP responses; never serialize raw driver errors.

## Tests and CI

Normal feature-enabled tests include configuration validation, redaction, and a
bounded connection-attempt test that requires no database:

```sh
cargo test -p xecute --features postgres,testing --test postgres
```

Live integration tests are explicitly ignored in the default suite. They fail
with a clear message if explicitly invoked without `TEST_DATABASE_URL`; they do
not silently pass when no database is available.

```sh
# Use the disposable instance from the example setup; its role can CREATE DATABASE.
export TEST_DATABASE_URL="$DATABASE_URL"
cargo test -p xecute --features postgres,testing --test postgres -- --ignored
```

Each live test creates its own database with a generated name, closes its pools,
and drops only that database. The configured role requires `CREATEDB`; use a
dedicated local/CI instance. The supplied database is used only for provisioning.
If a test panics, discard the disposable PostgreSQL instance afterward.

Coverage includes persistent repository writes, parameter binding, audit atomicity,
commit, explicit and dropped rollback, migration ordering, idempotency, checksum
mismatch, concurrent migration locking, failed-startup cleanup, acquisition limits,
readiness, closed-pool behavior, module DI, and HTTP injection. The repository's
`postgres` CI job runs the live suite against a PostgreSQL service.

SQLx reference: [pool options](https://docs.rs/sqlx/latest/sqlx/pool/struct.PoolOptions.html),
[migrations](https://docs.rs/sqlx/latest/sqlx/migrate/struct.Migrator.html),
[transactions](https://docs.rs/sqlx/latest/sqlx/struct.Transaction.html), and
[parameter binding](https://docs.rs/sqlx/latest/sqlx/fn.query.html).

## Keep learning

[Guards and JWT authentication](skills/xecute/references/integrations/auth.md). Return to the [learning path](skills/xecute/references/index.md) whenever you need a different topic.

# Guards and JWT authentication

Documentation route: /docs/integrations/auth

Protect selected routes using verified identities. Configure a trusted token verifier before adding role or permission checks; reading an Authorization header is not authentication.

Xecute supports executable guards at application, module, controller, and HTTP-method
scope. Guards run before request DTO extraction and handler execution. Optional
JWT authentication installs a verified principal; role and permission policies
then authorize that principal.

Enable the runtime's `auth` feature in your application:

```toml
[dependencies]
xecute = { version = "0.1", features = ["auth"] }
```

Custom guards require no feature flag. JWT verification, `AuthenticatedUser`,
`#[roles]`, and `#[permissions]` require `auth`. Existing MVC/CQRS resources remain
public until you attach guards. Generators do not create a login or user table.

## Choose the scope: module, controller, or route

Use `#[guard(...)]` with async guard functions. A guard receives a request and
returns `Result<Request, E>`, where `E` implements `IntoResponse`. Returning an
error stops the request before DTO validation and handler execution.

This custom guard checks a header; JWT verification is shown later in this guide:

```rust
use xecute::{HttpError, HttpStatus, middleware::Request};

async fn require_api_key(request: Request) -> Result<Request, HttpError> {
    // Example policy only: load real credentials from validated configuration.
    if request.headers().get("x-api-key").is_none() {
        return Err(HttpError::new(HttpStatus::UNAUTHORIZED));
    }
    Ok(request)
}
```

The example only checks presence. Do not use header presence as credential
verification; verify the value against your configured policy or use the JWT guard.

### Guard every controller in a module

In a generated MVC user module, add the annotation **below** `#[module(...)]`:

```rust
use xecute::{module, guard};
#[module(
    providers = [UserRepository, UserService, UserController],
    controllers = [UserController],
    exports = [UserService],
)]
#[guard(require_api_key)]
pub struct UserModule;
```

This is a module fragment: keep the generated imports for your providers and
import the guard function from its owning module. An equivalent declaration is
`#[module(..., guards = [require_api_key])]`; use either style. Multiple guards
run in list order. If both forms are used, `guards = [...]` runs first, followed
by the `#[guard]`, `#[roles]`, and `#[permissions]` annotations in source order.

Newly generated resources mount through `UserModule::scoped_router(...)`, so the
module policy covers every controller in its `controllers` list. Imported modules
are mounted separately; an import controls DI visibility, not HTTP ownership.

For manual routing, merge the **module** router instead of individual controllers:

```rust
let router = axum::Router::new()
    .merge(UserModule::scoped_router(container.clone()));
```

The `container` is an `Arc<Container>` built from all required module definitions.
Request-scoped DI context is installed before module guards, so a guard can resolve
providers through `RequestScope`. Controller types must still be registered as
providers; the `controllers` list does not replace provider registration.

### Guard one controller

```rust
use xecute::prelude::*;
#[controller("/user")]
#[guard(require_api_key)]
#[derive(Injectable)]
pub struct UserController {}
```

This fragment protects every route in the controller. Use it when other
controllers in the same module should have different policies.

### Guard one route

Inside the controller’s `#[routes]` implementation:

```rust
#[get("/private")]
#[guard(require_api_key)]
async fn private(&self) -> &'static str {
    "Allowed"
}
```

A route guard protects that HTTP method only. Other methods on the same path
keep their own policies. Module/controller guards still apply to every matched
path in their scope, including method-not-allowed requests. Unmatched paths and
separately merged public modules do not inherit another module’s policy.

### Combine scopes and JWT policies

```text
Application middleware → Application guards → Module guards
→ Controller middleware → Controller guards
→ Route middleware → Route guards → DTO extraction → Handler
```

Policies are additive. A route cannot bypass a guard on its controller or module.
Keep login/public routes in a separately mounted public module when necessary.
Module `#[roles(...)]` and `#[permissions(...)]` are supported with the `auth`
feature, just like controller and route policies. Authentication must run before
those checks, for example `#[guard(xecute::auth::authenticate_injected)]` followed
by `#[roles("admin")]` on the module. Configure the verifier provider first.

To guard every generated application route, place `#[guard(...)]` beneath the
root `AppModule`’s `#[module(...)]`. Its generated router applies the root guards
after assembling all resource modules, with DI context outside the guard layer.

### Existing applications

Updating the CLI does not rewrite previously generated routing code. Replace
`UserController::scoped_router(container.clone())` merges with
`UserModule::scoped_router(container.clone())` for each feature. In the root
`router_with_container` helper, after all feature merges, return:

```rust
Ok(xecute::with_container(AppModule::apply_guards(router), container))
```

Apply each module wrapper once, before merging unrelated routes. Calling a
controller router directly does not discover or apply its module’s guards.

## Run the example

From the repository root, generate a development secret and start the server:

```sh
export JWT_SECRET="$(openssl rand -hex 32)"
cargo run -p xecute --example auth --features auth
```

In another terminal, export the **same** development secret, then:

```sh
# The token subcommand is a local demo issuer, not a login endpoint.
ADMIN_TOKEN=$(cargo run --quiet -p xecute --example auth --features auth -- token admin)
READER_TOKEN=$(cargo run --quiet -p xecute --example auth --features auth -- token reader)

curl -i http://127.0.0.1:3000/health
# 200: public route
curl -i http://127.0.0.1:3000/users/me
# 401 + WWW-Authenticate: Bearer
curl -i http://127.0.0.1:3000/users/me -H "Authorization: Bearer $READER_TOKEN"
# 200: verified subject and roles
curl -i http://127.0.0.1:3000/users/admin -H "Authorization: Bearer $READER_TOKEN"
# 403: authenticated, missing admin role
curl -i http://127.0.0.1:3000/users/admin -H "Authorization: Bearer $ADMIN_TOKEN"
# 200: admin role and users:read permission
```

Tokens issued by the example expire after ten minutes. Never use the demo issuer
as production authentication: real issuance must authenticate credentials first.
The server binds only to localhost; use HTTPS at your production ingress.

## Configure a trusted verifier

```rust
use std::sync::Arc;
use axum::Extension;
use xecute::auth::JwtVerifier;

let secret = std::env::var("JWT_SECRET")?;
let verifier = Arc::new(JwtVerifier::hs256(
    secret.as_bytes(), "https://issuer.example", "users-api",
)?);
// Apply to the final router so authentication guards can read the verifier:
let router = router.layer(Extension(verifier));
```

HS256 requires at least 32 bytes of secret material; length alone does not imply
entropy, so generate it cryptographically and store it in a secret manager.
Shared-secret verifiers also possess signing capability. For externally issued
credentials, pin a trusted RS256 public key instead:

```rust
let verifier = JwtVerifier::rs256(
    &std::fs::read("./keys/access-token-public.pem")?,
    "https://issuer.example", "users-api",
)?;
```

Use an appropriately sized RSA key (at least 2048 bits). Key material is loaded
from trusted application configuration. The verifier does not fetch URLs or trust
`jku`, `jwk`, `x5u`, or token-supplied key material. `kid` does not select another
key; this API pins one key. JWKS fetching and automatic key rotation are not
included. Rotate configuration explicitly and plan overlapping validity through
your identity provider and application deployment.

Both constructors require nonblank issuer and audience. Verification pins the
algorithm and checks signature, expiration, issuer, and audience. `exp`, `iss`,
`aud`, and a nonblank string `sub` are required. An audience can be a string or a
list containing the configured audience. Optional `nbf` is checked. Clock leeway
is zero; keep issuer and server clocks synchronized. Unknown critical JOSE
extensions and tokens longer than 16 KiB are rejected. `iat`, token revocation,
and OAuth token-type semantics are not additional policies in this wrapper.
Use a dedicated API audience so tokens intended for another application are not
accepted here.

The supported authorization claim shape is:

```json
{
  "sub": "user-42",
  "iss": "https://issuer.example",
  "aud": "users-api",
  "exp": 2000000000,
  "roles": ["member", "admin"],
  "permissions": ["users:read", "users:write"]
}
```

`roles` and `permissions` are optional arrays of strings and default to empty.
Malformed claim types are rejected. Custom identity-provider claims, nested roles,
and OAuth's space-delimited `scope` are not automatically mapped. Use trusted
issuer configuration or an application-specific authentication guard to adapt
those formats; never create authorization data from unsigned request input.

## Protect controllers and routes

```rust
use xecute::prelude::*;
use xecute::auth::{self, AuthenticatedUser};

#[controller("/users")]
#[guard(auth::authenticate)]
#[roles("member")]
#[derive(Injectable)]
pub struct UserController {}

#[routes]
impl UserController {
    #[get("/me")]
    async fn me(&self, user: AuthenticatedUser) -> String {
        user.0.subject().to_owned()
    }

    #[post("")]
    #[roles("admin")]
    #[permissions("users:write")]
    async fn create(&self) -> &'static str {
        "Authorized"
    }
}
```

Place controller annotations **below** `#[controller]` on the struct. You can
alternatively put controller policies below `#[routes]` on the impl. Route
annotations belong inside the owning `#[routes]` impl on HTTP handlers. Using
these annotations outside their owning macro is a compile error. Legacy
`#[controller("...")] impl ...` syntax is supported as well.

All listed roles and all listed permissions are required, with exact,
case-sensitive matching. There is no implicit admin bypass, wildcard expansion,
or OR policy. Module, controller and route policies are additive: a route cannot weaken
its enclosing scopes' requirements. Empty policies are compile errors (and direct
runtime helper calls deny empty lists). For OR policies or record ownership,
write a custom guard or domain authorization service.

Authentication must execute before role/permission guards. Keep
`#[guard(auth::authenticate)]` above policies in the same scope. `AuthenticatedUser`
only reads an already verified principal; it does not silently parse credentials.
The principal exposes subject, roles, permissions, expiry, `has_role`, and
`has_permission`. Its fields are private and it cannot be deserialized from user
input. Authorization of a specific record still belongs in your application after
loading that record: a users:read permission alone does not establish ownership.
Reuse those checks for HTTP, command handlers, and background jobs.

## Application guards and public routes

```rust
let router = xecute::Application::new(router)
    .use_guard(xecute::auth::authenticate)
    .into_router()
    .layer(axum::Extension(verifier));
```

Application guards protect the entire supplied router, including fallback
responses. To keep health, login, or public endpoints unauthenticated, prefer
guarding only protected controllers or merge a guarded private router with a
separate public router afterward. There is no `#[public]` annotation that bypasses
an already-running application/controller guard. Avoid broad URI-prefix bypasses
inside authentication code.

Controller guards preserve unrelated 404 routes. A method-level guard does not
protect another HTTP method on the same path and does not replace that method's
405 response. Policy changes do not silently add guards to newly generated
controllers: explicitly protect each private controller, or use a global guard.

## Custom guards and dependency injection

A guard is an async function taking the request and returning it on success:

```rust
use xecute::{HttpError, HttpStatus, middleware::Request};

async fn require_feature(request: Request) -> Result<Request, HttpError> {
    let enabled = request.extensions().get::<bool>().copied().unwrap_or(false);
    if !enabled { return Err(HttpError::new(HttpStatus::FORBIDDEN)); }
    Ok(request)
}
```

Attach it with `#[guard(require_feature)]` or
`Application::use_guard(require_feature)`. Multiple guards execute in declaration
order; the first rejection prevents subsequent guards, DTO decoding/validation,
and handler execution. A guard can enrich request extensions but must leave the
body untouched. Return safe error types; custom guard responses are application
code, so Xecute cannot redact arbitrary text you put into them.

For DI-managed authentication, register `JwtVerifier` as a provider value and use
`#[guard(auth::authenticate_injected)]` on a controller built with `scoped_router`.
The guard resolves the verifier through the active `RequestScope`; missing
configuration or failed DI resolves to a safe 500. Export/import the provider's
owning module when sharing it across modules.

Custom guards can resolve services via
`request.extensions().get::<xecute::RequestScope>()` and `scope.resolve::<T>()`.
Module/controller/route guards created by `scoped_router` already have a request scope.
For a global DI guard, install `xecute::with_container(router, container)` **outside**
the assembled Application router, so the scope exists before the guard executes.
With direct `Controller::router`, use the Extension-backed verifier or install
`with_container` explicitly. Existing async lifecycle providers must complete
`initialize_async()` before traffic reaches any guard.

## Execution order

Xecute uses nested router scopes. At each scope, middleware runs before guards:

```text
Application middleware → application guards
  → root module guards → feature module guards
    → controller middleware → controller guards
      → route middleware → route guards
        → request extraction/DTO validation → handler
```

Middleware registration and guard registration are each ordered independently;
calling `use_guard` before `use_middleware` still runs application middleware
first. A controller can attach middleware/policies to both its struct and impl;
then struct scope wraps impl scope, which wraps route scope. This is Xecute's
explicit nesting order; it does not promise NestJS's separate, universal
all-middleware-then-all-guards lifecycle. Install CORS/preflight handling outside
authentication when browsers need unauthenticated OPTIONS handling.

## Errors, OpenAPI, and boundaries

- Missing/malformed/duplicate Authorization headers, invalid tokens, and missing
  principals return 401 with `WWW-Authenticate: Bearer`.
- A valid principal lacking a role/permission returns 403.
- An absent configured verifier returns a safe 500; it never grants access.

Bearer scheme matching is case-insensitive; this implementation requires exactly
one Authorization header and one non-whitespace token. It accepts no query-string
or cookie token fallback. Error bodies use Xecute's safe JSON envelope; wrap your
router with `exceptions::exception_boundary` for request IDs and normalization.
Neither token values, JWT verification reasons, nor key material appear in these
errors. Do not log Authorization headers or bearer tokens in custom middleware.

Guard annotations do not yet add bearer security schemes to generated OpenAPI.
When preparing Swagger documents, add a `components.securitySchemes.bearerAuth`
entry with `type: http`, `scheme: bearer`, and `bearerFormat: JWT`, then add
`security: [{"bearerAuth": []}]` only to protected operations. Document 401/403
responses with existing `#[resp]` annotations. Public operations should remain
explicitly public in the document.

This feature verifies bearer access tokens and applies application policies.
Password registration/login, password hashing, refresh tokens, sessions/cookies,
CSRF protection, logout/revocation, OAuth/OIDC discovery, and tenant/record-level
policies remain separate application/identity-provider responsibilities. Role
changes are reflected when the issuer issues new claims or your application
checks a current policy store; previously issued tokens remain valid until expiry
unless you implement revocation. No authentication storage is auto-generated.

## Tests

```sh
# Core custom guards, without JWT dependencies:
cargo test -p xecute --no-default-features --test guards_http

# Real signature verification, HTTP policy/extractor tests, and runnable demo tests:
cargo test -p xecute --features auth --test auth_http --test guards_http --example auth

# Reject invalid macro policy declarations:
cargo test -p xmacros
```

Tests cover HS256/RS256, wrong keys and algorithms, algorithm confusion,
unsigned/malformed/expired/not-yet-valid tokens, required issuer/audience/subject,
malformed role/permission claims, header ambiguity, safe errors and correlation,
public endpoints, additive policies, body validation ordering, scoped DI, global
and legacy guard execution, and preservation of unrelated methods/paths. PEM
files under `tests/fixtures/auth` are generated **test-only** keys.

Implementation references: [jsonwebtoken verification/validation](https://docs.rs/jsonwebtoken/latest/jsonwebtoken/struct.Validation.html)
and [jsonwebtoken key and crypto backend documentation](https://github.com/Keats/jsonwebtoken).

## Keep learning

[Jobs and scheduling](skills/xecute/references/integrations/jobs.md). Return to the [learning path](skills/xecute/references/index.md) whenever you need a different topic.

# Jobs and scheduling

Documentation route: /docs/integrations/jobs

Move suitable work out of a request handler into bounded workers. These jobs run in the current process and are not durable across restart; choose that model before configuring retries.

Enable Xecute's `jobs` feature for bounded, process-local Tokio workers with
receipts, retries, per-attempt deadlines, graceful draining, and interval schedules.

```toml
[dependencies]
xecute = { version = "0.1", features = ["jobs"] }
```

This feature does not require a broker or database. **Accepted jobs are not persisted:** a process crash/restart loses
queued and running work. Use a durable broker or a database outbox/worker system
for work that must survive a crash. This implementation is suitable for bounded
best-effort application work; it does not claim exactly-once delivery, distributed
leases, dead-letter storage, or multi-process queue coordination.

## Create a queue and observe completion

```rust
use std::time::Duration;
use xecute::jobs::{JobContext, JobError, JobQueue, QueueConfig};

struct SendEmail { user_id: u64 }

let config = QueueConfig::new(128, 4)?
    .retry(3, Duration::from_millis(250))?
    .attempt_timeout(Duration::from_secs(10))?;

let queue = JobQueue::new(config, |job: JobContext<SendEmail>| async move {
    // Pass job.id to your delivery API as an idempotency key when supported.
    // Call an async email client using job.payload.user_id here.
    let _ = (job.id, job.attempt, job.payload.user_id);
    Ok::<(), JobError>(())
})?;

let receipt = queue.enqueue(SendEmail { user_id: 42 }).await?;
let job_id = receipt.id();
let outcome = receipt.wait().await?;
assert_eq!(outcome.id, job_id);
assert!(outcome.result.is_ok());
queue.shutdown().await?;
```

`JobQueue::new` must run inside an active Tokio runtime with its time driver
enabled. `JobQueue::provider` defers startup until the container's async startup
and attaches a queue-draining shutdown hook. Queue clones share workers, buffer,
shutdown state, and counters; they do not create additional worker pools.

`JobContext<T>` contains an `Arc<T>` payload, stable UUID, and one-based attempt
number. Payloads need `Send + Sync + 'static`, but do not need `Clone`. A receipt
waits for this particular accepted job; dropping its receipt does not cancel the
job. No unbounded in-memory job history is retained, and an ID alone cannot be
used to look up an old result. Retain/observe receipts or record application job
state when clients need later status checks.

## Backpressure, limits, and retries

`QueueConfig::new(capacity, workers)` requires positive capacity and 1..=1024
workers. Capacity is the maximum **waiting** job count; up to `workers` additional
jobs can be running. Payload size is application-controlled; choose appropriate
payload bounds as well as a buffer count. Retry delay occupies a worker slot,
preventing a failing dependency from creating an unbounded retry backlog.

- `enqueue(payload).await` waits for capacity; cancellation before it returns
  means the payload was not accepted.
- `try_enqueue(payload)` returns `QueueError::Full` immediately when capacity is
  exhausted, and `Closed` after shutdown starts.
- A failed submission consumes its payload; retain a clone/application record
  yourself if you intend to submit again.

Defaults are three total attempts, 100ms fixed delay, and a 30-second deadline per
attempt. `.retry(max_attempts, delay)` supports 1..=100 total attempts; zero delay
is valid. `.attempt_timeout(duration)` requires a positive, representable duration.

Handlers return:

```rust
Err(JobError::Retryable("temporary_delivery_error"))
// or
Err(JobError::Permanent("recipient_invalid"))
```

Only `Retryable` errors and timeouts are retried, up to the configured attempt
count. Permanent errors stop immediately. Handler panics become a terminal
`JobFailure::Panicked`; they do not kill the queue's other workers or cause an
automatic retry. Rust's ordinary panic hook still controls panic logging, so do
not panic with secrets or request payloads. Use static, safe diagnostic codes in
`JobError` values.

`JobOutcome` reports `attempts` and `result`, with permanent, retry-exhausted,
timed-out, and panicked terminal states. A receipt returns `WorkerStopped` if its
worker is aborted before delivering an outcome. `stats()` exposes submitted,
succeeded, failed, and retried counters as process-local approximate snapshots.
Terminal failures are not automatically stored or published; observe outcomes
and emit application logs/metrics deliberately.

On timeout, the attempt task is aborted and joined before retrying. Cancelling a
Rust future does not undo a remote operation that already committed. Use the same
`job.id` across retries as an idempotency key, and apply application/database
uniqueness guarantees where required. CPU-heavy or blocking code prevents prompt
cooperative cancellation; workers are for nonblocking async handlers. `spawn_blocking`
work and external side effects require their own cancellation/lifetime policy.

## Dependency injection and resource ordering

For a handler without DI dependencies:

```rust
let definition = JobQueue::provider(config, |job: JobContext<SendEmail>| async move {
    let _ = job.payload.user_id;
    Ok::<(), JobError>(())
});
let container = xecute::Container::builder().provider(definition).build()?;
container.initialize_async().await?;
let queue = container.resolve::<JobQueue<SendEmail>>()?;
// Submit work.
container.shutdown_async().await?;
```

When handlers depend on a database, cache, or client, use your own
`ProviderDefinition::singleton_async::<JobQueue<YourJob>, _, _>` factory. Declare
all `ProviderKey` dependencies, resolve them from its supplied container, and
capture their Arcs in the handler. Attach
`.on_shutdown::<JobQueue<YourJob>, _, _>(...)` to await `queue.shutdown()`.
This dependency graph makes queues drain **before** databases/caches close.
Do not resolve the queue back into its own handler: that creates an ownership
cycle and can prevent final-drop cancellation.

The runnable [jobs/cache example](https://github.com/morshedulmunna/xecute/blob/main/xecute/examples/jobs_cache/main.rs) implements this
pattern with `Cache` as an explicit queue dependency, a retryable job, and cleanup
even when application work fails:

```sh
cargo run -p xecute --example jobs_cache --features jobs,cache
```

Controllers can inject `Arc<JobQueue<YourJob>>` or extract it with `Inject<T>` in a
scoped router. Prefer small payloads containing stable record IDs. Do not copy
Authorization headers, request scopes, or borrowed HTTP request data into jobs.
Background jobs have application-owned lifetime, not HTTP request lifetime.
Authorize the request before enqueueing, and perform any current record-level
policy checks your job requires when it executes.

Each payload type identifies one concrete DI provider. Use distinct payload/newtype
wrappers for independent queues. Module imports/exports and test overrides follow
the existing container rules. With the `testing` feature, queues work with
`TestingModule::compile_async()`.

## Graceful shutdown and cancellation

`shutdown().await` stops submissions, rejects blocked producers, drains already
accepted jobs including retries, and joins all workers. Calls are safe concurrently
or repeatedly. `is_closed()` reports whether submissions have stopped. Never call
shutdown from one of the same queue's handlers: shutdown waits for that handler.

Stop HTTP submission sources and interval schedules first, then drain requests
and queues, then close their dependencies. Estimate a drain deadline from queue
capacity, worker count, attempt limits, retry delays, and actual handler behavior.
There is no implicit queue-wide shutdown timeout.

If a caller cancels `queue.shutdown()`, join handles remain owned by the queue;
calling it again resumes draining. Dropping all queue handles aborts its workers
and their currently executing attempt tasks. That is cancellation, not graceful
completion. If you put an external timeout around `Container::shutdown_async`,
remember the lifecycle system does not retry a cancelled cleanup hook: retain a
queue handle if you need to resume its drain explicitly.

## Interval schedules

```rust
let mut schedule = queue.schedule_every(Duration::from_secs(60), || {
    SendEmail { user_id: 42 }
})?;
// Keep the handle alive while the schedule is wanted.
let skipped = schedule.skipped();
schedule.stop().await?;
queue.shutdown().await?;
```

The first occurrence is after one full interval, not immediately. Missed ticks use
Tokio's `Skip` policy. A full queue skips that occurrence and increments
`skipped()` rather than accumulating jobs. A closed queue stops the schedule.
Schedule creation does not wait for individual job results; observe queue failure
counters and instrument the handler. The payload factory must be short and
nonblocking. `is_finished()` reveals an exited scheduling task, and `stop()`
reports an unexpected task/factory panic as `WorkerStopped`. Stop is idempotent;
dropping the handle aborts future ticks but does not cancel already accepted jobs.

Schedules are per-process: four replicas run four schedules. Distributed singleton
cron, persisted schedules, cron expressions, time zones, and leader election are
not included. To lifecycle-manage a schedule, put its handle behind a Tokio mutex
in its own singleton provider, declare the queue as its dependency, and stop the
handle in its shutdown hook. This orders schedule stop before queue draining.

## Tests

```sh
cargo test -p xecute --features jobs,cache,testing --test jobs --test cache --example jobs_cache
```

Queue tests cover retry identity/delay, permanent and exhausted failures, timeout
cancellation, panic isolation, bounded concurrency/capacity, cancelled submissions,
dropped receipts, shutdown draining/cancellation/resumption, final-drop task
ownership, scheduling timing/full-queue behavior, schedule factory failures, and
DI cleanup order. Time-dependent unit tests use Tokio's paused clock.

Reference: [Tokio task ownership and cancellation](https://docs.rs/tokio/latest/tokio/task/struct.JoinHandle.html)
and [interval missed-tick behavior](https://docs.rs/tokio/latest/tokio/time/enum.MissedTickBehavior.html).

## Keep learning

[Memory and Redis caching](skills/xecute/references/integrations/cache.md). Return to the [learning path](skills/xecute/references/index.md) whenever you need a different topic.

# Memory and Redis caching

Documentation route: /docs/integrations/cache

Cache data that can be recomputed, with an explicit key and expiration. Start with memory caching; use Redis only when you need that backend and have a Redis service available.

Xecute exposes an explicit `Cache` API for JSON values or bytes, positive TTLs,
exact-key invalidation, and lifecycle cleanup. Choose bounded process-local memory
or an optional namespaced Redis backend. Caching is opt-in; no controller response
or authenticated data is cached automatically.

Enable the feature in your application's Cargo.toml:

```toml
[dependencies]
xecute = { version = "0.1", features = ["cache"] }
# Use features = ["cache-redis"] for Redis; this also enables cache.
```

## Memory cache

```rust
use std::time::Duration;
use xecute::cache::Cache;

let cache = Cache::memory(1000, 1_048_576)?;
cache.set("catalog:v1:product:42", &serde_json::json!({"name":"Keyboard"}),
    Duration::from_secs(60)).await?;
let product = cache.get::<serde_json::Value>("catalog:v1:product:42").await?;
cache.delete("catalog:v1:product:42").await?;
cache.close().await?;
```

The first limit is entry count; the second is maximum **serialized bytes per
value**. Both must be positive. Keys must be nonempty and at most 512 bytes.
Capacity bounds stored entries, while application limits bound the working input
and serialization allocation. Memory overhead includes keys and bookkeeping in
addition to value bytes. This small cache uses a mutex and linear LRU bookkeeping;
use Redis or a specialized application cache when workloads require larger/highly
contended local caches.

Expired entries are removed lazily on reads/writes/deletes. When capacity is full,
a new key evicts the least recently read/written live entry. An overwrite replaces
both value and expiration; reads refresh LRU position **without** extending TTL.
Clones share entries. Separate application processes do not share memory entries,
and all entries disappear on restart or explicit memory-cache closure.

## API semantics

- `set(key, &value, ttl)` JSON-serializes a value. `get::<T>(key)` returns
  `Option<T>`; misses and expired entries return `None`.
- `set_bytes` / `get_bytes` support raw byte data.
- `delete(key)` invalidates only that key and returns whether a live entry existed.
- `close()` is shared and idempotent. Future operations return `Closed`; memory
  entries are cleared, while Redis entries retain their normal server TTL.

Every set requires a positive TTL. Zero, overflowing, or unrepresentable durations
return `InvalidTtl`; persistent entries are not created accidentally. Redis TTLs
are rounded **up** to whole milliseconds; memory uses the monotonic Tokio clock.
Backend writes apply value and TTL atomically within that backend. A rejected
oversized value or invalid TTL does not replace an old entry.

JSON decoding/type mismatches return `Serialization`, not `None`. Keep key schemas
versioned when changing serialized types. Use an `Option` field or a tagged value
when your domain needs to distinguish a cached null/negative result from a miss.
Errors are static and redacted. Redis failures return `Unavailable`, distinct from
a cache miss. Decide whether your application should recompute, fail, or use a
separate fallback policy; do not silently hide every storage/serialization error.

## Redis configuration

Use a dedicated local instance to try the Redis backend:

```sh
docker run --detach --rm --name xecute-redis-demo \
  -p 127.0.0.1:56379:6379 redis:8
export TEST_REDIS_URL='redis://127.0.0.1:56379/'
cargo test -p xecute --features cache-redis --test cache_redis -- --include-ignored
docker stop xecute-redis-demo
```

Configure application Redis separately from test credentials:

```rust
use std::time::Duration;
use xecute::cache::{Cache, RedisCacheConfig};

let config = RedisCacheConfig::new(
    &std::env::var("REDIS_URL")?, "users-api-v1",
)?
.max_value_bytes(1_048_576)?
.timeout(Duration::from_secs(2))?;
let cache = Cache::redis(config).await?;
cache.set("tenant:7:user:42", &42, Duration::from_secs(60)).await?;
let value = cache.get::<u64>("tenant:7:user:42").await?;
cache.close().await?;
```

URLs may use `redis://` or TLS `rediss://`. Store credentials in environment/secret
management; debug output redacts connection options and runtime errors exclude
URLs and driver messages. For networked production Redis, configure authenticated
ACLs and verified TLS; do not disable certificate verification via URL options.

The namespace is 1..=128 ASCII letters, digits, dots, underscores or hyphens.
Physical keys are `namespace:key`; clients using the same Redis database and
namespace share entries, while different namespaces remain separate. Namespace
isolation is a naming convention, not an authorization boundary: scope Redis ACLs
and infrastructure access appropriately. Xecute never calls FLUSHDB, FLUSHALL, or
wildcard deletion. Individual deletes affect only the selected namespaced key.

The stable Redis client provides multiplexing/reconnection. Initial connection
and each complete operation, including waiting on reconnection, have a configured
positive timeout (default two seconds). A timed-out network command may already
have reached Redis; it is not a transactional undo guarantee. Reconnection is not
a durable write queue. Values written by another application may still allocate
memory while being received before this wrapper can reject an oversized value;
use a cache-owned namespace and server-side memory limits as well.

Redis capacity/eviction is controlled by the server (`maxmemory` and its eviction
policy), not the memory-cache entry limit. Redis persistence, clustering,
replication/failover and availability are operational choices outside this
wrapper. Closing a handle drops its connection manager after outstanding clones
finish; it deliberately leaves shared entries untouched.

## Cache-aside and invalidation

Use explicit application caching after authorization:

```text
Controller → authorize user/record → Service or Query Handler
  → Cache lookup → hit: return value
                 → miss: Repository → cache result with TTL → return value
```

Include tenant, user/ownership scope, representation/version, locale, filters and
pagination wherever they affect a result. For example,
`v1:tenant:7:user:42:orders:page:1` must not become a shared `orders` key across
users. Do not cache authentication decisions, raw bearer tokens, or secrets using
these examples. Never allow a cache hit to bypass the guard/record-level policy
checks added in step 3.

After a successful database write, invalidate affected keys. Cache/database writes
are not one transaction; handle failed invalidation and concurrent stale readers
with your application's consistency strategy (for example versioned keys or an
outbox). TTL alone provides eventual expiration, not strict read-after-write
consistency. No automatic get-or-load/single-flight locking, stampede protection,
HTTP cache interceptor, or cross-backend transaction is provided.

## Dependency injection and lifecycle

```rust
let cache = Cache::memory_provider(1000, 1_048_576)?;
// Redis alternative: Cache::redis_provider(redis_config)
let container = xecute::Container::builder().provider(cache).build()?;
container.initialize_async().await?;
let cache = container.resolve::<Cache>()?;
// Use the cache, drain callers/jobs, then:
container.shutdown_async().await?;
```

Memory provider registration creates the value immediately, but its cleanup hook
still requires async container lifecycle. Redis connects at async startup. Module
registration, exports/imports and isolated testing overrides work as before.
Register one `Cache` provider; use concrete newtype adapters if a feature needs
multiple independent caches in the same container.

Repositories/services/query handlers can depend on `Arc<Cache>`. Workers must
declare `ProviderKey::of::<Cache>()` in their queue factory so lifecycle shutdown
drains the queue before closing the cache. See the
[jobs/cache example](https://github.com/morshedulmunna/xecute/blob/main/xecute/examples/jobs_cache/main.rs):

```sh
cargo run -p xecute --example jobs_cache --features jobs,cache
```

Generated MVC/CQRS resources are not automatically rewritten to use caching. In
generated servers, use the async initialization path described in the
[lifecycle guide](skills/xecute/references/architecture/lifecycle.md), then
retain the container for cleanup after HTTP requests and workers drain.

## Tests and CI

```sh
# No external service needed:
cargo test -p xecute --features cache --test cache

# Redis config/timeout tests, without a live server:
cargo test -p xecute --features cache-redis --test cache_redis

# Explicit live Redis suite:
TEST_REDIS_URL=redis://127.0.0.1:56379/ \
  cargo test -p xecute --features cache-redis --test cache_redis -- --ignored
```

Memory tests cover exact expiry, non-sliding TTL, overwrite, LRU eviction, lazy
expiry before eviction, serialization/type/size errors, concurrent access,
invalidation, and lifecycle closure. Time tests use Tokio's paused clock.
Redis tests cover separate clients, namespace isolation, server TTL/overwrite,
JSON/size errors, wrong-type command failures, connection timeouts, redaction,
and cleanup that preserves shared entries.

Live tests are ignored by default, but explicitly invoking them without
`TEST_REDIS_URL` fails with an actionable message. Tests use random namespaces and
never flush Redis or alter unrelated keys. The dedicated Redis CI job runs these
checks against a disposable service.

Reference: [Redis SET with expiration](https://redis.io/docs/latest/commands/set/)
and [Redis async connection management](https://docs.rs/redis/latest/redis/aio/struct.ConnectionManager.html).

## Keep learning

[CQRS buses and events](skills/xecute/references/integrations/cqrs.md). Return to the [learning path](skills/xecute/references/index.md) whenever you need a different topic.

---

# CQRS buses and events

Documentation route: /docs/integrations/cqrs

Use typed buses when you want central command/query dispatch or event subscribers. Generated CQRS already works through direct handler injection; adding buses is a separate application choice.

Xecute's optional `cqrs` runtime feature provides typed `CommandBus`, `QueryBus`,
and `EventBus` registries. Commands/queries dispatch to one handler; events fan
out to zero or more subscribers. All three share ordered pipeline behaviors,
explicit dispatch metadata, ordinary DI module validation, and caller-owned async
execution.

Enable the feature in your application's Cargo.toml:

```toml
[dependencies]
xecute = { version = "0.1", features = ["cqrs"] }
```

The feature does not start a worker, open a database, require a broker, or spawn
hidden tasks. These are in-process application buses, not a distributed messaging
transport. CQRS does not require separate databases, event sourcing, or buses for
every small application. Existing direct-handler CQRS generation remains valid.

## Run the HTTP example

From the repository root:

```sh
cargo run -p xecute --example cqrs --features cqrs

# In another terminal:
curl -i -X POST http://127.0.0.1:3000/users \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{"name":"  Munna  "}'
curl -i http://127.0.0.1:3000/users
```

The [example](https://github.com/morshedulmunna/xecute/blob/main/xecute/examples/cqrs/main.rs) separates controller, DTO, entity,
repository, command/query handlers, event subscribers, module registrations and a
shared pipeline policy. The write handler normalizes/validates a name, persists a
user, then publishes `UserCreated` to audit and welcome subscribers. The query
handler reads the same repository. Welcome handling records a demo action; it does
not send email. Storage is bounded in-memory demonstration data, not durable user
or audit storage. The HTTP example is public; add the [authentication guards](skills/xecute/references/integrations/auth.md)
when protecting a real API.

```text
POST → DTO → Controller → CommandBus → Behaviors → CreateUserHandler → Repository
                                                    └→ EventBus → Audit / Welcome
GET  → Controller → QueryBus → Behaviors → ListUsersHandler → Repository
```

## Typed commands and queries

A command declares its output and domain error; a handler supplies an async
implementation. Queries have the same shape using `Query` / `QueryHandler`.

```rust
use std::{convert::Infallible, sync::Arc};
use xecute::cqrs::{Command, CommandHandler, CommandBus, DispatchContext};

struct Add { value: u64 }
impl Command for Add {
    type Output = u64;
    type Error = Infallible;
}

struct AddHandler;
impl CommandHandler<Add> for AddHandler {
    async fn handle(&self, command: Add, _: DispatchContext)
        -> Result<u64, Infallible>
    {
        Ok(command.value + 1)
    }
}

let commands = CommandBus::builder()
    .handler::<Add, _>(Arc::new(AddHandler))
    .build()?;
let result = commands.execute(Add { value: 41 }).await?;
assert_eq!(result, 42);
```

For closures/functions, use `.handler_fn::<Add, _, _>(|command, context| async move
{ ... })`. Messages must be `Send + Sync + 'static`; outputs/errors must be
`Send + 'static`. A message does not need `Clone`. A concrete Rust message type
identifies its handler; strings and serialized type names are not routing keys.
Command and query registries are separate. Their traits express intent; the query
trait does not technically prevent application code from writing to a database.

Exactly one handler per command/query type is allowed. Duplicates fail `build()`
or `into_provider()` instead of silently replacing a handler. Dispatch of an
unregistered message returns `BusError::MissingHandler` before behaviors run.
Registries are immutable after construction and safe to clone/share concurrently.
A bus clone shares the same registered handler instances.

### Error mapping

`execute` returns `Result<Output, DispatchError<YourError>>`:

- `DispatchError::Handler(error)` preserves the handler's typed domain error.
- `DispatchError::Bus(error)` represents registration/routing/pipeline failure.

Map these deliberately at your HTTP boundary. For example, a known duplicate
resource can become 409, a validation failure 422, and an unexpected bus failure
500. Do not serialize arbitrary domain errors or call their Display output in a
public HTTP response. Bus errors contain static codes/type names, but internal
configuration/type details still should not be exposed as client diagnostics.
There is no automatic HTTP status mapping for arbitrary CQRS errors.

## Dependency injection and module boundaries

Register handlers with the ordinary DI container, then bind them to a bus:

```rust
use xecute::{ModuleDefinition, Scope};
use xecute::cqrs::CommandBus;

let commands = CommandBus::builder()
    .handler_provider::<Add, AddHandler>()
    .into_provider(Scope::Singleton)?;

// Register AddHandler using its Provider definition, or a concrete value:
let module = ModuleDefinition::new("math")
    .provider(xecute::ProviderDefinition::value(AddHandler))
    .provider(commands);
```

Build `ModuleGraph` as usual and initialize the container before serving. Resolve
or inject `Arc<CommandBus>` and call it from a controller/service. The runnable
example uses `#[derive(Injectable)]` for its controller and handlers. Configured
buses are registered with their builder's `into_provider`, not by putting bare
`CommandBus` / `QueryBus` / `EventBus` types into `#[module(providers = [...])]`.
Those types cannot infer application-specific registrations on their own.

`handler_provider` and `behavior_provider` add declared dependencies to the bus's
provider definition. Existing missing-provider, module import/export, cycle and
scope validation applies. A handler or behavior in another module must be exported
and its owning module imported by the bus's module. Missing providers fail graph
construction; resolution/factory errors fail bus construction/startup.

Bindings resolve handlers **once when the bus is constructed**, not on each
execute. The resulting bus retains handler Arcs, not a `Container`; this avoids
container → singleton cache → bus → container reference cycles. Singleton buses
can retain only compatible provider scopes. For request-scoped handlers, register
the bus with `Scope::Request` and resolve it through the active `RequestScope` or
`scoped_router` / `Inject<CommandBus>`. Different request buses then retain their
own request handler instances while sharing permitted singleton dependencies.
A transient handler bound into a singleton bus is retained for that bus's lifetime;
use a request/transient bus when new handler instances per resolution are needed.

For manual binding, `.build_with(&container)` uses an existing root container;
`.build_in(&request_scope)` uses one request scope. `.build()` is for direct
Arc/closure registrations and reports `ProviderContextRequired` if a DI-backed
registration has no binding context. Direct Arc/closure captures are app-owned
objects; their dependency lifetimes cannot be inferred or validated by the bus.

Async handler dependencies from step 1 work normally: call `initialize_async()`
before routing traffic. Stop in-flight dispatches before calling container
shutdown and closing their database/cache dependencies. Buses do not add a
separate lifecycle hook or detach handler work. A handler Arc can outlive its
container when retained elsewhere; do not execute it after its resources close.

The legacy `Injector` can resolve an explicitly registered `.value(bus)`; it does
not synthesize an empty bus. Native `Container` / `ModuleGraph` is preferred for
configured buses and provider lifetimes.

## Explicit dispatch context

```rust
#[derive(Clone)]
struct CorrelationId(String);

let context = DispatchContext::default()
    .with_value(CorrelationId("request-123".into()));
let result = commands.execute_with(Add { value: 41 }, context).await?;
```

`context.value::<CorrelationId>()` reads typed metadata. Context clones share Arc
values but have independent maps, so replacing a value on a cloned context does
not modify another dispatch's metadata map. Values with interior mutability still
follow their own synchronization rules. Context Debug output reports only value
count and does not print payloads.

HTTP principals, request IDs, transactions and cancellation tokens are not
implicitly propagated. Extract the verified `AuthenticatedUser` or server-issued
request ID, then pass the required trusted values explicitly. Do not put raw
bearer tokens or an entire HTTP request into dispatch context. Reusable command
handlers must enforce business invariants for non-HTTP callers too; controller
DTO validation alone does not protect job/CLI/event entry points.

## Shared pipeline behaviors

A `Behavior` wraps a continuation for a registered command/query or complete event
publication. Register outer-to-inner order with `.behavior(Arc::new(...))` or
`.behavior_provider::<YourBehavior>()`.

```rust
use xecute::cqrs::{Behavior, BusError, DispatchFuture, Next};

struct RequireCorrelation;
impl Behavior for RequireCorrelation {
    fn handle<'a>(&'a self, next: Next<'a>) -> DispatchFuture<'a> {
        Box::pin(async move {
            if next.context().value::<CorrelationId>().is_none() {
                return Err(BusError::Rejected("correlation_required"));
            }
            let response = next.run().await?;
            let succeeded = response.is_success();
            // Record duration/result metadata without logging submitted payloads.
            let _ = succeeded;
            Ok(response)
        })
    }
}
```

`Next` exposes `info()` (Command/Query/Event and concrete type),
`message::<YourMessage>()`, and `context()`. `next.run()` consumes the continuation,
so downstream execution is invoked at most once through that continuation.
Behaviors can validate/authorize, reject, inspect a typed payload before
continuing, or inspect the result afterward. This order is verified:

```text
first before → second before → handler → second after → first after
```

A handler's domain failure is still a completed pipeline response;
`response.is_success()` is false. For typed inspection, use
`response.value::<Result<Output, DomainError>>()`. Event responses instead contain
`EventReport`, and success is false if any subscriber failed. A pipeline rejection
or panic returns a `BusError` without a normal response. As with ordinary async
code, code after `next.run().await?` does not run when that await returns an error;
match the result explicitly when cleanup/logging must cover failures.

A trusted behavior may intentionally short-circuit with
`DispatchResponse::from_result::<Output, DomainError>(Ok(cached_value))` or
`from_event_report(report)`. The final bus checks the concrete response contract;
returning the wrong result type fails with `InvalidResponse`. Only implement
caching for query types/authorization scopes where it is correct. A typed bus
pipeline is not an HTTP guard and does not automatically apply JWT policies.

Behaviors have no automatic retry or transaction wrapper. Retrying an entire
command or a whole event publication can repeat side effects. A SQL transaction
must be owned/passed explicitly by application handlers or transaction-aware
adapters; there is no implicit transaction propagation through DispatchContext.

## Event fan-out and observable failures

```rust
use std::sync::Arc;
use xecute::cqrs::{Event, EventBus, EventError};

struct UserCreated { id: String }
impl Event for UserCreated {}

let events = EventBus::builder()
    .handler_fn::<UserCreated, _, _>("audit", |event, _| async move {
        let _ = event.id.as_str();
        Ok::<(), EventError>(())
    })
    .handler_fn::<UserCreated, _, _>("welcome", |_, _| async move {
        Err(EventError::Handler("email_unavailable"))
    })
    .build()?;
let report = events.publish(UserCreated { id: "user-42".into() }).await?;
assert_eq!(report.attempted, 2);
assert_eq!(report.succeeded, 1);
assert!(!report.is_success());
```

For structs, implement `EventHandler<E>` and use `.handler::<E, H>(Arc<H>)` or
`.handler_provider::<E, H>()`. Each subscriber receives an `Arc<E>` and an explicit
context; one publication shares the same event payload across subscribers. No
`Clone` implementation is required on the event. Subscriber names must be
nonblank and unique **within one event type**. Direct typed subscribers use the
concrete handler type name; closures use their explicit name. Duplicate names are
startup/build errors.

Subscribers run sequentially in registration order. A returned `EventError` or
unwinding panic is collected in `EventReport.failures`, and later subscribers
still run. Reports contain attempted/succeeded counts and ordered named failures.
A publication with no subscribers is a successful empty report. Behaviors wrap
the whole publication; a rejecting behavior can prevent fan-out entirely.

`publish(...).await` completes only after subscriber work finishes. It does not
mean queued delivery and does not automatically create a background job. There
are no implicit subscriber retries, deadlines, dead-letter records or persistent
subscriptions. If delivery must be asynchronous, explicitly enqueue work using
[jobs](skills/xecute/references/integrations/jobs.md), and remember that step 4's queue is also process-local.

Ordinary unwinding panics during handler/behavior execution are converted to safe
bus/event failure results. The default Rust panic hook still runs and may log the
panic text; do not panic with secrets. `panic = "abort"`, process failures and
panicking destructors are not recoverable delivery guarantees. Recovery does not
undo state changes or repair a poisoned/mutated application resource.

## Write consistency, workflows, and sagas

Publish domain events deliberately after successful repository persistence. A
failed subscriber does **not** roll back a committed write or earlier subscriber
side effects. In the example, the user remains created even if event delivery is
incomplete; delivery failure is reported separately instead of returning a false
"creation rolled back" result.

A crash between commit and publish can lose notifications. Use a transactional
outbox in PostgreSQL plus a durable delivery worker when notifications must survive
that gap. Neither the in-process EventBus nor the process-local JobQueue provides
an outbox, exactly-once execution or event sourcing. Persist idempotency state and
use stable event/operation IDs when retrying side effects.

An event subscriber can coordinate a follow-up command through an explicitly
supplied command bus. Keep dependencies acyclic: if a command handler depends on
EventBus and an event subscriber depends on the same CommandBus containing that
handler, ModuleGraph correctly rejects the circular dependency. Use a separate
newtype-wrapped follow-up command registry, explicit orchestration, or a durable
outbox boundary rather than hiding the cycle with a retained Container.
Long-running persisted sagas, compensation state machines, broker transports,
aggregate event stores and replay are not implemented by this feature.

## Cancellation and deadlines

Execution futures remain owned by the caller. Cancelling an execute drops its
current handler/pipeline future; cancelling event publication leaves completed
subscriber side effects intact and drops the current subscriber before later
subscribers run. No internal task continues work in the background. Application
handlers can still spawn their own tasks, so their ownership is your responsibility.

There is no automatic deadline. Use your HTTP request timeout or an explicit
`tokio::time::timeout` when appropriate. Timeout/cancellation is not a transaction
rollback guarantee for already completed database/remote operations. Apply the
same idempotency and cleanup rules as other async application code.

## Adopt in generated MVC/CQRS applications

`xecute g resource user` still emits direct
`Controller → Command/Query Handler → Repository` calls in CQRS mode. Existing
features are not rewritten automatically, and the CLI currently does not enable
this runtime feature or create bus registries by default. Adoption is explicit:

1. Enable the runtime's `cqrs` feature, using the local runtime path until release.
2. Implement `Command`/`Query` and their handler traits for existing command/query
   types. A trait handler can delegate to your existing `.execute(...)` method.
3. Add handler-provider registrations to the configured buses and add their
   `into_provider(...)` definitions to the owning ModuleDefinition. Export/import
   dependencies as required.
4. Inject `Arc<CommandBus>` / `Arc<QueryBus>` into the controller and map
   `DispatchError` to safe HTTP/domain responses.
5. Register event subscribers and explicitly publish at the chosen write boundary.

Use the complete example's module/controller code as the reference. MVC services
may also call buses; choosing a bus does not require moving every operation into
CQRS. Keep HTTP DTOs under `dto/` and domain/application messages under
`commands/`, `queries/` and `events/`.

## Tests

```sh
cargo test -p xecute --features cqrs,testing --test cqrs --example cqrs
cargo check -p xecute --no-default-features
```

Tests cover typed outputs/domain errors, duplicate/missing handlers, pipeline
ordering/short circuits/response validation, command/query/event metadata, event
fan-out and panic continuation, empty/unrelated subscriptions, DI visibility,
request scope isolation, provider overrides, invalid dependency cycles, absence of
container reference cycles, concurrent contexts, caller cancellation, and the HTTP
controller → buses → handlers → repository → subscribers example.

Reference: [NestJS CQRS concepts](https://docs.nestjs.com/recipes/cqrs) and
[FutureExt unwind handling](https://docs.rs/futures-util/latest/futures_util/future/trait.FutureExt.html).

# Quality checks

Documentation route: /docs/testing/checks

Run these commands from the generated application root before shipping a change. The page distinguishes application checks from checks for contributors working on Xecute itself.

In a generated application:

```sh
cargo fmt --all -- --check
cargo clippy --all-targets --all-features --locked -- -D warnings
cargo test --all-targets --all-features --locked
cargo build --release --locked
```

New standalone projects resolve dependencies with `cargo generate-lockfile` during
setup, including `--runtime-path` projects. This selects the latest stable versions
within the template’s compatibility ranges, instead of copying a bundled lockfile.
Registry access is required unless Cargo is configured for offline cached resolution.
Resolution failures return an error and preserve generated files; fix registry/network
access and rerun `cargo generate-lockfile` in the project. Commit `Cargo.lock` for
reproducible builds. Breaking major upgrades require updated templates. Existing
workspace apps retain shared dependency versions when adding another app; setup
does not force upgrades across an existing workspace.

Resource HTTP tests verify rejection before persistence and visibility of created
records through subsequent reads. Server tests cover configuration, quota and
concurrency behavior, timeouts, body limits, response envelopes, CORS, request IDs,
logging, and Swagger routes. The workspace middleware tests cover scope ordering,
early returns, validation boundaries, and compatibility with legacy controllers.

The generator also includes CI, rustfmt/Clippy configuration, EditorConfig,
Dependabot configuration, and `deny.toml`. To run the dependency policy check:

```sh
cargo install cargo-deny --locked
cargo deny --locked check
```

Document public items with `///` and modules with `//!`. Missing documentation
produces compiler warnings; Clippy CI treats warnings as errors.
